motions.title: SD3: Integrating the Department of Public Health - Substance Abuse Prevention and Control (DPH-SAPC) within the Homeless Services System
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Public Health Substance Abuse Prevention and Control to report back in 120 days on integrating substance use disorder services within the homeless services system. It also directs a report back in 30 days on establishing a senior executive position to coordinate homeless programs across departments.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
HAHN  
__________________________ 
 BARGER 
 __________________________ 
SOLIS 
__________________________ 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH   
    
  December 1, 2026  
Integrating the Department of Public Health - Substance Abuse Prevention and 
Control (DPH-SAPC) within the Homeless Services System 
Los Angeles County continues to face an urgent homelessness and public-health 
crisis. The 2026 Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count estimated that approximately 
73,040 people were experiencing homelessness countywide, including approximately 
49,002 people living unsheltered. Demographic data further indicates that approximately 
one in four adults experiencing homelessness reports a substance use disorder, 
underscoring the need for accessible services that reach people on the streets, in interim 
housing, and after they enter permanent housing. 
Substance use and homelessness are interconnected through a range of structural 
and individual vulnerabilities. Losing housing increases the risks associated with 
substance use, and people with untreated behavioral-health conditions, trauma histories, 
and poverty are disproportionately vulnerable to becoming homeless. Once homeless, 
the persistent trauma that comes from living without a home, fragmented care, untreated 
substance use disorder, overdose risk, and gaps between levels of treatment make it 
substantially more difficult for people to obtain and retain stable housing. Drug and alcohol 
overdose remained the leading cause of death among people experiencing 

homelessness in 2024, accounting for approximately 40 percent of deaths. Although the 
overdose mortality rate declined by 21 percent that year, it remained 46 times higher 
among people experiencing homelessness than among the overall County population. 
The Department of Public Health’s Substance Abuse Prevention and Control 
Bureau (DPH-SAPC) leads and facilitates the County’s publicly funded system of 
substance use prevention, harm reduction, treatment and recovery services, and 
administers the County’s Drug Medi-Cal Organized Delivery System (DMC-ODS). 
Effective care for people experiencing homelessness requires close integration between 
this system and the Department of Homeless Services and Housing (HSH), including 
coordinated outreach, low-barrier engagement, harm reduction, medications for addiction 
treatment, timely placement across the appropriate levels of care and continuity during 
transitions between the streets, treatment, and housing. 
The Board of Supervisors approved the “Better Reaching the 95%” motion on 
October 17, 2023, in recognition that only approximately 5% of people with substance 
use disorder access treatment, while the remaining 95% may not believe they need 
treatment, may not be ready to seek care, may encounter barriers that make traditional 
treatment difficult to access, or may be disillusioned with the models of treatment they 
have tried. The motion directed County departments to build upon DPH-SAPC’s Reaching 
the 95% initiative (R95) by strengthening outreach, lowering barriers to treatment, 
connecting homeless-service providers to substance use resources, engaging Medi-Cal 
managed care plans, and identifying and connecting individuals who need substance use 
services but are not accessing them.   

DPH-SAPC has also used payment reform to deploy provider capacity building 
and value-based incentives which have expanded the reach of Los Angeles County’s 
contracted substance use treatment provider network to adopt lower barrier, person-
centered practices and improve engagement, care coordination, and continuity of care. 
The DPH-SAPC treatment system has increased LA County residential beds by over two-
fold, increased receipt of residential services over ten-fold, increased Recovery Bridge 
Housing (RBH) beds by over 12.5-fold, saw a four-fold increase in the number of clients 
served in intensive outpatient services, and saw a 200-fold increase in addiction 
medication services beyond methadone since the implementation of the DMC-ODS 
waiver in 2017.  DPH-SAPC has increased the percentage of clients in Los Angeles 
County who are seeking substance use treatment for the first time to over 40% of clients 
admitted to care, demonstrating an increasing reach of substance use treatment to 
eligible people in Los Angeles County. Reaching individuals who are not already 
connected to the specialty substance use disorder system requires coordination between, 
and reducing barriers facing people served by, several existing systems, including those 
managed by DPH-SAPC, the Department of Mental Health (DMH), HSH, healthcare 
providers, community-based organizations, and Medi-Cal managed care plans. 
  
Coordination between DPH-SAPC and HSH must continue to be strengthened.  
Support for people experiencing homelessness should include navigation assistance, 
alignment of assessments, coordination with payors to reduce disputes, and access to 
shelter, housing, healthcare, and long-term stability. 
 

I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Department of 
Public Health Substance Abuse Prevention and Control (DPH-SAPC), in consultation with 
the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and the Department of Homeless Services and 
Housing (HSH), to report back to the Board in writing in 120 days, and biannually 
thereafter, to consolidate and align with the “Reforming and Integrating Mental Healthcare 
within the County’s Homeless Services System” motion report.  The report should include, 
but not be limited to the following, as well as any barriers, and staffing or funding that may 
be needed: 
1. Designate additional staff responsible for collaborating with HSH, the 
Department of Mental Health (DMH), Los Angeles Health Services Department 
(LAHS), and other relevant County Departments, on programs for people 
experiencing homelessness. The report should include information on the 
identification of the appropriate DPH items needed to designate and assign 
staff to address the subsequent directives. The collaboration should focus on 
people with lived experience, providers, harm-reduction organizations, cities 
and local jurisdictions, hospitals, community clinics, correctional partners, and 
other stakeholders to determine barriers to access, effectiveness of funded 
treatment models and providers, and innovative solutions to support people’s 
journey to healing.  
2. Examine opportunities to expand access to Substance Use Disorder (SUD) 
services as a component of HSH services, the Emergency Centralized 
Response Center (ECRC), interim-housing sites, access centers, permanent 
housing programs, hospitals, other healthcare delivery systems, and other high-

volume locations engaging with and serving people experiencing homelessness 
through consultation, technical assistance, and co-located DPH-SAPC-funded 
services.  
3. DPH-SAPC, in consultation with DMH, LAHS, HSH, and County Counsel, 
should also report back on how to strengthen planning, and establish 
coordinated protocol plans between DPH-SAPC, DMH, LAHS, and HSH for 
programs and funding affecting people experiencing homelessness with 
substance use needs, including Behavioral Health Bridge Housing funding, 
Behavioral Health Services Act funding, Opioid Settlement Funding, Measure A 
funding, Drug Medi-Cal funding, and other state, federal, or local resources. The 
plans should include a description of how clinical and programmatic information 
will be shared, including but not limited to health information exchange, joint 
case consultation, coordinated service planning, and clear assignment of 
responsibility so that disputes concerning diagnosis, level of care, payer, or 
departmental responsibility do not delay services. 
4. Engage local Medi-Cal managed-care plans in coordination with HSH, LAHS, 
and DMH to ensure shared understanding amongst all parties on the 
responsibilities to strengthen connections to Enhanced Care Management, 
Community Supports, non-specialty behavioral-health care, primary and 
specialty healthcare, and other covered benefits for people experiencing 
homelessness. 
5. Report back on the overdose prevention recommendations included in Public 
Health’s Center for Health Impact Evaluation’s Mortality Rates and Causes of 

Death Among People Experiencing Homelessness in Los Angeles County 
report. 
6. The Better Reaching the 95 Percent motion future reports should be 
consolidated with the report back for this directive, with an enhanced focus on 
directives from this motion specific to services and coordination for the needs of 
People Experiencing Homelessness (PEH). 
7. Review, strengthen, and standardize implementation of existing DPH-SAPC 
discharge and transition-of-care requirements, including Reaching the 95% 
(R95) discharge policy, to ensure individuals leaving treatment receive a 
documented warm hand off to appropriate services. The review should include, 
where feasible, a closed-loop process that confirms referral acceptance of 
successful connections to housing and/or services. Additionally, ensure that 
community-facing staff from DPH-SAPC and its contracted provider network 
understand the full HSH housing and shelter continuum and can make effective 
connections to those resources. 
8. Identify opportunities to expand field-based screening, engagement, care 
coordination, initiating and continuing addiction medications, (also known as 
medications for addiction treatment), contingency management, and additional 
clinically appropriate services in locations where people experiencing 
homelessness are found, including encampments, vehicles, shelters, interim 
housing, correctional facilities, and permanent-supportive-housing sites, 
through field-based services, interim-housing programs, bridge clinics, primary 
care, correction health, emergency departments, hospitals and coordinated 

referrals. The report should include what additional resources are necessary to 
advance this directive.  
9. Continue to assess and identify state legislative changes that are needed to 
support the delivery of substance use services to people experiencing 
homelessness impacted by substance use. 
10. Identify and implement metrics for tracking the progress and outcomes of the 
directives outlined above.  
I, FURTHER, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct DPH-SAPC, in 
consultation with the CEO and HSH, to report back to the Board in writing in 30 days on 
identifying and developing a senior DPH executive position that reports to the Director of 
the Department of Public Health and will be  responsible for collaborating with HSH, the 
Department of Mental Health (DMH), Los Angeles Health Services Department (LAHS), 
and other relevant County Departments, on programs for people experiencing 
homelessness. The DPH executive will also be responsible for coordinating services and 
programs to more effectively integrate across the Department to develop a unified 
response to homelessness.  The DPH Executive will have experience working with people 
experiencing homelessness and/or lived experience of homelessness.  The report should 
include the classification, cost, and potential sources of funding, included but not limited 
to Behavioral Health Services Administration (BHSA), Measure A, HUD Continuum of 
Care (COC), and state homeless funding. 
#          #          # 
LPH:aa

motions.title: SD3: Transitional Housing Program (TRP) Round 8, Housing Navigation and Maintenance Program (HNMP) Round 5, and THP-Plus Housing Supplement Program Round 6.
motions.summary: Approve a resolution authorizing the Department of Children and Family Services to accept state funding for transitional housing and navigation programs for foster youth. Direct the department to execute contract and memorandum of understanding amendments to distribute the funding to expand housing capacity and navigation services.

MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL

___________________________

AGN. NO.             
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH  
December 1, 2026 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Transitional Housing Program (TRP) Round 8, Housing Navigation and 
Maintenance Program (HNMP) Round 5, and THP-Plus Housing Supplement 
Program Round 6 
 
California’s high housing costs have led to housing instability and homelessness. 
This reality is felt most by young people, including those who are or have been in foster 
care. Housing instability is critical to the pursuit of higher education, meaningful 
employment, and self-sufficiency for youth as they transition to adulthood. 
As this Board has noted time and again, when young people exit foster care, it can 
be challenging to find resources and housing opportunities; and when there are 
resources, they are often limited in number.  Transitional Housing Program Plus (THP-
Plus) is one such program that has expanded in recent years at the direction of the Los 
Angeles County Board of Supervisors and the hard work of the Department of Children 
and Family Services (DCFS).  THP-Plus has been a critical housing program for youth 
ages 18-25 years old who were formerly in foster care.  THP-Plus services play a critical 
role in supporting former foster youth as they transition to adulthood by providing stable 

 
 
housing and supportive services that promote self-sufficiency, educational attainment, 
and employment. As housing costs continue to rise and the needs of transition-age youth 
become increasingly complex, expanding access to THP-Plus is essential. Increased 
collaboration among DCFS, the Department of Economic Opportunity (DEO), Department 
of Mental Health (DMH), Department of Public Social Services (DPSS) and other County 
partners can strengthen connections to workforce development, education, and 
behavioral health.  
The State of California Department of Housing and Community Development 
issued an allocation acceptance form dated September 10, 2026, under Round 8 of the 
Transitional Housing Program (“THP”), authorized by item 2240-102-0001 of section 2.00 
of the Budget Act of 2026 (Chapter 19 of the Statutes of 2026) and Chapter 11.7 
(commencing with section 50807) of part 2 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code 
(the “THP Allocation Acceptance Form”). 
The State of California Department of Housing and Community Development 
issued an Allocation Acceptance form dated September 10, 2026, under Round 5 of the 
Housing Navigation and Maintenance Program (“HNMP”) authorized by item 2240-103-
0001 of section 2.00 of the Budget Act of 2026 (Chapter 19 of the Statutes of 2026) and 
Chapter 11.8 (commencing with section 50811) of Part 2 of Division 31 of the Health and 
Safety Code (the “HNMP Allocation Acceptance Form”). 
The State of California Department of Housing and Community Development 
issued an allocation acceptance form dated September 10, 2026, under Round 6 of the 
THPSUP Housing Supplement program authorized by item 2240-102-0001 of Section 
2.00 of the Budget Act of 2026 (Chapter 19 of the Statues of 2026) and Chapter 11.9 

 
 
(commencing with HSC 50820) of Part 2 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code 
(collectively, the “Statue”) (the “THP Plus SUP Allocation Acceptance Form”).  
The Housing Navigation and Maintenance Program will be administered by 
participating counties to fund Housing Navigators to act as housing specialists for young 
adults ages 18 and up to 24 years of age and will assist with securing and maintaining 
housing. Priority will be given to young adults in the foster care system. In addition, Los 
Angeles County may use the funding to provide housing navigation services directly or 
through a contract with other housing assistance programs in the County.  
The THP allocations will be shared among participating counties for the purpose 
of housing stability to help young people ages 18 to 25 years old secure and maintain 
housing through THP-Plus. With the growing population of TAY, DCFS is monitoring the 
need to expand housing and supportive services capacity for specialized young adult 
populations, prioritizing the development of beds and services tailored to those requiring 
specialized supports and interventions based on data and forecasted such as but not 
limited to pregnant and parenting youth. This is a critical opportunity and Los Angeles 
County must leverage it to support youth previously in foster care.   
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that in order to participate in the State of California THP 
Round 8, HNMP Round 5, and THP-Plus Housing Supplement Round 6 funding 
allocations, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors: 
1) Approve the attached resolution authorizing DCFS to participate in the THP 
Round 8, HNMP Round 5, and THP-Plus Housing Supplement Round 6 and 
accept the additional funding allocation. 

 
 
2) Instruct the Interim Director of DCFS, or designee, to accept the funding for 
the THP Round 8, HNMP Round 5, and THP-Plus Housing Supplement Round 
6 for Los Angeles County, by submitting the signed resolution to the California 
Department of Housing and Community Development. 
3) Delegate authority to the Interim Director of DCFS, or designee, in consultation 
with County Counsel, to execute amendments to THP-Plus contracts to 
increase the Maximum Contract Sum to distribute the new funding allocation 
to accommodate an increase in units of service and/or increase the current 
rate of the units, and to update THP-Plus contracts for necessary 
programmatic changes. Execution of amendments is contingent upon: a) 
County Counsel approval being obtained prior to execution of such 
amendments, and b) DCFS notifying the Board and the Chief Executive Officer 
(CEO) in writing, within 10 business days of such amendment. 
4) Instruct the Interim Director of DCFS, or designee, in consultation with County 
Counsel, to execute amendments to the Memorandum of Understanding 
(MOU) between DCFS and the Department of Homeless Services and 
Housing (HSH) for Housing Navigators to increase the MOU amount with the 
new funding allocation. 
 
#             #             #

motions.title: SD-3 • “Protecting Communities Vulnerable to Fire Risk and Climate Hazards by Implementing the Recommendations of the Blue- Ribbon Commission on Climate Action and Fire Safe Recover” for December 01, 2026 Board Agenda
motions.summary: Directs the Rebuild Authority, County Fire, and other departments to implement recommendations from the Blue-Ribbon Commission on Climate Action and Fire Safe Recovery. Directives include evaluating the creation of a Fire Control District, developing a home hardening program, reducing invasive plants, and launching a philanthropic rebuilding fund.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
 
MITCHELL 
  _________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
  _________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 _________________________ 
 
BARGER 
 _________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
  _________________________ 
 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH                          December 1, 2026 
Protecting Communities Vulnerable to Fire Risk and Climate Hazards by 
Implementing the Recommendations of the Blue-Ribbon Commission on Climate 
Action and Fire Safe Recovery 
The January 2025 Wildfires were the most devastating disaster in Los Angeles 
County history.  The Palisades and Eaton fires claimed more than 18,000 structures and 
thousands of families and businesses are still displaced two years later.  The same 
dangerous conditions that caused those fires also caused nearly a dozen other wildfires 
over those two weeks, threatening hundreds of thousands of people in multiple 
communities.  Los Angeles County has been designated by FEMA as the county prone 
to the most natural hazards of any county in the United States, and more than a million 
Angelenos reside in the Wildland-Urban Interface, with heightened exposure to wildfire.  
California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment found that the total area that burns in 
wildfires each year will increase by 50% by mid-century without changes in land 
management, primarily attributed to native chapparal becoming stressed and replaced by 
grasses and other fire-prone invasive plants. 
 

In February 2025, the Third Supervisorial District convened an independent Blue-
Ribbon Commission on Climate Action and Fire Safe Recovery (BRC) to assess lessons 
learned from the fires and to develop forward-looking policy recommendations to support 
a resilient, equitable, and sustainable region. Funded in part by a grant from the California 
Community Foundation, the Commission was intentionally established as an independent 
body, operating outside of County departments, to provide expert-driven and community-
informed recommendations that could guide policy decisions at every level of 
government. Commission members included local and national experts across disaster 
response, economic development, water, energy, land use, finance, insurance, public 
health, and housing. The Commission was supported by a multidisciplinary, world-class 
research team at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to ground its work in 
rigorous analysis, data, and global best practices. In June 2025, the BRC presented their 
final report including 59 recommendations to local and state officials, including 
suggestions to keep other similarly vulnerable communities safe from future disasters. 
In February 2026, the Board of Supervisors directed the Chief Sustainability Office 
(CSO) to evaluate the conclusions of the BRC, document the County’s progress in 
implementing those recommendations, and suggest actions that merit further 
implementation.  The CSO, with the assistance of many departments, presented their 
findings in a July 2026 report and presentation.  They concluded that 18 months after the 
fires, a majority of the BRC recommendations had been at least partially implemented.  
This is a noteworthy accomplishment, given the fact that this is the first major disaster in 
modern US history without public assistance or long-term recovery aid from the federal 
government. One notable accomplishment was the creation of LA County’s Disaster 

Recovery Rebuild Authority (RA). The BRC’s top recommendation was the creation of a 
Rebuild Authority that could cross jurisdictional lines and support an accelerated and 
streamlined recovery.  The RA has been launched within LA County Public Works as the 
unified coordinating body for disaster recovery with the mission of rebuilding fire-impacted 
unincorporated communities with speed, accountability, and resilience.  Many of the BRC 
recommendations underway are at various levels of implementation through the RA. 
The second overarching governance recommendation of the BRC was the creation 
of a Fire Control District (FCD), to mitigate risks from wildfires and work to protect the 
many   homes and businesses in Los Angeles County facing risk from wildfire.  In 2020, 
voters in Marin County approved the creation of the Marin Wildfire Prevention Authority 
(MWPA), funded by a parcel tax.  The MWPA funds community emergency 
preparedness, home hardening resiliency retrofits, and community infrastructure that 
reduces fire risk.  The BRC recommendation suggested that this FCD could serve all Los 
Angeles County parcels (akin to other countywide measures), though it could feasibly be 
narrowed to only include communities served by the LA County Fire Department 
(LACoFD), unincorporated communities, or properties within defined wildland-urban 
interfaces.  Home hardening retrofits could be led by LA County’s Internal Services 
Department (ISD), which has experience implementing hundreds of millions of dollars 
worth of private building energy retrofits through its Southern California Renewable 
Energy Network (SoCalREN). ISD submitted applications to the Federal Emergency 
Management Agency (FEMA) to fire harden and retrofit several hundred vulnerable 
homes near the Eaton and Palisades Fire burn scars but is awaiting the release of federal 
funds to implement these and other fire recovery assistance programs. 

A related set of BRC recommendations concern the twin objectives of reducing 
future fire risk by restoring fire-vulnerable ecosystems with native plants.  The CSO 
prioritized a recommendation that the County develop and seek funding for a program to 
remove invasive plants on public lands that present fire risk, particularly in areas 
recovering from wildfires, and other high-priority areas.  Recent initiatives in this space 
include: 
• LACoFD received grants from Prop 4 (the Climate Bond) to reduce fire risks 
through various strategies on land owned by the Mountains Recreation 
Conservation Authority (MRCA).   
• The Agricultural Commissioner/Weights and Measures (AC/WM) regularly 
inspects private property and clears hazardous vegetation and brush as part of 
the County’s Weed Abatement Program.   
• The Department of Parks and Recreation (Parks) is leading a successful 
ecological restoration of the County-operated Eaton Canyon Nature Center, 
including a robust workforce development program.   
• The Department of Regional Planning (Planning) is finalizing a Community 
Wildfire Protection Ordinance, for new developments, to address adequate 
evacuation egress during wildfire events, to improve public safety, and reduce 
risks to development located within the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones.   
Planning is also finalizing a Countywide Community Wildfire Protection Plan to 
prioritize and better compete for resources to address fire risks to existing 
communities 
• Following a March 2026 motion, Planning and LA County Fire Department have 

been preparing an additional study for a Regional Wildfire Mitigation Joint 
Powers Authority for the Santa Monica Mountains, to cost-share wildfire risk 
mitigation strategies, which could provide an early model for how a 
collaborative fire mitigation program could work. 
While the County continues to advocate for overdue federal resources, there is 
more we can do to leverage funding to assist our communities, building on initiatives 
underway.  The County created Disaster Recovery Financing Districts for the Santa 
Monica Mountains and Altadena to redirect local property tax revenue back into those 
communities.  The County is preparing a Long-Term Recovery Plan to guide resilient 
recovery, infrastructure investment, and future programs to assist fire survivors.  
Philanthropy has provided support for community recovery, and as we approach two 
years without federal assistance, there is a pronounced need for philanthropy to help 
bridge the gap.  The BRC recommended the creation of a “LA Resilient Rebuilding and 
Reconstruction Fund,” to provide a coherent vision and investment plan for philanthropic 
support to reduce barriers to community desires to rebuild with resiliency. In a similar 
vein, and thanks to Los Angeles County’s advocacy, the California Public Utilities 
Commission released funding for the RISE (Rebuilding Incentives for Sustainable 
Electric) Homes incentive program, which provides a financial incentive for wildfire 
survivors to rebuild sustainably.  Additional permanent funding sources should be 
identified so that all communities around California can be prepared to rebuild safer and 
more resiliently following future disasters.   
As we approach the two-year anniversary of the 2025 wildfires, there is a need to 
advance additional long-term strategies to support resilient recovery and to effectively 

invest in wildfire-vulnerable communities across Los Angeles County. The BRC report 
remains a useful guide to direct long-term recovery and preparedness. 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1. Direct the Rebuild Authority to report back in each quarterly update to the Board 
on its plan to implement and track the progress of incorporating relevant Blue 
Ribbon Commission recommendations identified by the Chief Sustainability 
Office’s report that would help accelerate rebuilding, catalyze investment, and 
restore ecosystems.  The report should describe how those recommendations will 
be incorporated into the Rebuild Authority’s workplan, including which strategies 
will be prioritized with and without external resources. 
2. Direct the LA County Fire Department, in consultation with the CEO, Department 
of Regional Planning, Chief Executive Office, and Chief Sustainability Office, to 
report back in 120 days on the feasibility of creating a Fire Control District which 
would serve as a fire risk mitigation and preparedness entity for Los Angeles 
County.  The report should evaluate geographic options (i.e. LA County inclusive 
of incorporated cities, unincorporated LA County, specific wildland-urban 
interfaces) including analyses of revenue estimates, varying funding scales, 
anticipated costs, and initiatives that could be supported by a Fire Control District, 
akin to Marin County’s Wildfire Prevention Authority. 
3. Direct Internal Services Department to report back in 120 days on a proposal to 
create a home hardening program for properties located in high fire severity zones, 
including funding strategies, and scenarios for scaling the program. 

4. Direct County Fire and Agricultural Commissioner/Weights and Measures to join 
and participate in the State’s wildfire restoration working group and to report back 
to the Board in 180 days on strategies and funds needed to reduce proliferation of 
invasive plants on public lands that present a fire risk, in areas recovering from 
wildfires, and other high priority areas, starting with a pilot initiative in the Santa 
Monica Mountains. 
5. Direct CEO Legislative Affairs and Intergovernmental Relations Branch to: 
a. Advocate for an amendment to Executive Order N-29-25 to only allow 
exemptions to the energy code for those properties where legacy 
homeowners or next of kin are rebuilding, following the County’s own 
standards for applying fee deferrals to fire survivors; 
b. Support proposals to establish permanent and dedicated resilient rebuild 
incentives, beyond the existing authorized statewide CPUC RISE program.   
6. Direct the CEO to launch a LA Resilient Rebuilding and Reconstruction Fund 
philanthropic campaign to generate opportunities for philanthropy to support 
resilient rebuilding and community risk reduction.   
#          #          # 
LPH:ao,ss,ds

motions.title: SD3: Protecting Residents and Communities from Unlawful Practices at Non-Clinical Recovery Residences
motions.summary: Directs County Counsel, in consultation with relevant departments and community stakeholders, to report back in 120 days with a coordinated protocol for addressing alleged unlawful conduct by non-clinical recovery residences. The protocol must address complaint routing, referral safeguards, enforcement options, and resident protections during closures.

MOTION

HORVATH 
__________________________

__________________________

__________________________ 
 
 SOLIS 
 __________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH   
 
November 17, 2026 
Protecting Residents and Communities from Unlawful Practices at Non-Clinical 
Recovery Residences 
Recovery residences, commonly known as sober-living homes, are non-clinical 
housing sites that provide alcohol- and drug-free housing and peer support. They are an 
important bridge between treatment and independent living, providing stable recovery 
housing, especially for people leaving residential treatment, incarceration, hospitals, or 
homelessness.  The National Study of Treatment and Addiction Recovery Residences 
(NSTARR)’s 2022 longitudinal study estimated that Los Angeles had 1.02 recovery 
residences per 100,000 population, ranking at 24th in per capita availability out of the 58 
counties of California, suggesting concerningly low accessibility given the County 
population and projected housing needs.  When operating solely as housing, without 
treatment, detoxification, counseling, recovery planning, or other clinical services, these 
residences are not licensed, certified, or routinely investigated by the California 
Department of Health Care Services (DHCS). 
DHCS has sole authority to license adult residential substance use disorder 
recovery or treatment facilities that provide treatment services, and may investigate a 

recovery residence suspected of providing said services without a required state license. 
Other state agencies retain authority within their respective jurisdictions, (including the 
Attorney General), regarding unlawful or fraudulent business practices and employ state 
health care and insurance regulators overseeing the proper execution of health plan, 
insurance, and billing matters. However, California does not currently have a 
comprehensive statewide regulatory framework for recovery residences, creating an 
oversight gap that may be exploited by operators engaging in unsafe, fraudulent, or 
abusive practices.  These practices have historically included malfeasant providers billing 
insurance or Medi-Cal for services that were not provided; or intentionally providing 
substances to keep residents addicted in order to continue billing, and upon discovery of 
misconduct, operators have used multiple "shell" corporations to conceal ownership or 
avoid enforcement.  These are but a few examples of the bad acts perpetrated without 
oversight, many of which are capable of repetition, yet evading review.    
At the local level, there are several entities with various responsibilities connected 
to the regulation and oversight of recovery residences.  Within incorporated cities, each 
city is responsible, (either directly or through a contracted agency), for administering and 
enforcing applicable zoning, land-use, building, fire, business-licensing, property-
maintenance, labor, and nuisance laws.  Los Angeles County generally exercises 
comparable local authority in unincorporated areas, only. 
The Department of Public Health's Substance Abuse Prevention and Control 
division (DPH-SAPC) leads the County’s publicly funded system of substance-use 
prevention, treatment and recovery services, and administers the County’s Drug Medi-
Cal Organized Delivery System.  DPH-SAPC administers County contracts with both 

substance use disorder services providers, as well as with a small number of recovery 
residence providers; the latter also known as Recovery Bridge Housing (RBH) providers. 
DPH-SAPC monitors contractual agreements closely, with established standards, 
incident reports and can impose contractual remedies, if necessary.  However, DPH-
SAPC does not regulate privately operated recovery residences and can only monitor the  
subset of RBH providers who are directly contracted with DPH-SAPC. 
Although DPH-SAPC is the primary County contracting agency for RBH, other 
County departments, (e.g., the Department of Mental Health (DMH) or the Department of 
Homeless Services and Housing (HSH)), may refer individuals to recovery residences 
and are responsible for coordinating and overseeing their own referral process and 
addressing concerns related to those referrals.  Nonetheless, DPH-SAPC as well as DMH 
and HSH are under County jurisdiction collectively, and a ubiquitous approach to 
addressing this issue is obviously mutually beneficial for all parties.   
A coordinated, risk-based approach can improve accountability by using existing 
complaints, permitting, code-enforcement, contracting, consumer-protection, litigation, 
and law-enforcement authority; prioritizing serious and repeat offenders; and referring 
matters outside County jurisdiction to the appropriate state or municipal agency.  
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct County Counsel, in 
consultation with the Department of Public Health Substance Abuse Prevention and 
Control (DPH-SAPC), the District Attorney (DA), the Department of Consumer and 
Business Affairs (DCBA), Regional Planning (RP), Public Works (DPW), the Fire 
Department, the Sheriff's Department, other relevant County departments, and 
engagement with community stakeholders, including substance use providers and 

individuals with lived experience, report back in writing to the Board in 120 days with a 
coordinated, risk-based protocol for addressing alleged unlawful conduct by non-clinical 
recovery residences, within their respective jurisdictional authorities, including 
procedures for coordinating with and referring matters to the appropriate local, state, or 
federal enforcement authority. The protocol and any recommended options shall be 
consistent with the federal Fair Housing Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the 
California Fair Employment and Housing Act, and shall target unlawful conduct rather 
than the disability status of residents. The protocol should include, but not limited to the 
following: 
1. Complaint System: Provide details and recommendations to improve existing 
complaint systems that receive, document, and route allegations to the appropriate 
local, state, or federal enforcement authority. 
2. Safeguards for Referrals: Within existing resources, develop uniform safeguards 
for privately operated, recovery residences that County-operated and County-
contracted providers make referrals to.  
3. Enforcement: Analyze enforcement criteria and make recommendations to 
improve existing business, building, fire, zoning, property-maintenance, consumer-
protection, contracting, labor, and public-nuisance laws, as well as coordination 
with applicable state and federal enforcement authorities. This analysis should 
identify the jurisdiction and responsibilities of relevant agencies and recommend 
procedures for interagency coordination, information sharing, and referrals, 
including referral of suspected unlicensed recovery or treatment services to the 
California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) and referral of appropriate 

consumer-fraud, insurance-fraud, or criminal matters to the responsible 
enforcement authority.  The analysis should include, but not limited to the following: 
a. Escalating enforcement options, as legally appropriate; and 
b. Procedures to protect residents affected by an emergency closure or other 
enforcement 
action, 
including 
coordination 
of 
safe 
relocation, 
transportation, medication continuity, naloxone access, and connection to 
appropriate housing or treatment when necessary.  
4. Identify any additional options the County has at its disposal to regulate non-clinical 
recovery residences, including the pros and cons of those options. 
5. Outline actions that can be implemented within existing resources, any legal or 
operational gaps, and any staffing or funding needs requiring separate Board 
consideration. 
#          #          #

motions.title: SD2: Supporting Fresh Food Access at the Martin Luther King, Jr. Medical Campus
motions.summary: Directs the Chief Executive Officer to waive daily permit fees and negotiate a two-year, gratis license agreement with Sustainable Economic Enterprises of Los Angeles. This authorizes the continued operation of the Watts Willowbrook Farmers' Market at the Martin Luther King, Jr. Medical Campus.

- 
MORE - 
 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
 
HAHN

BARGER

SOLIS 
__________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL  
 
      
November 17, 2026 
Supporting Fresh Food Access at the Martin Luther King, Jr. Medical Campus 
Access to fresh, affordable food is essential to health, yet many communities 
continue to face significant barriers to obtaining nutritious produce. Residents of Service 
Planning Area (SPA) 6 experience the greatest barriers in Los Angeles County (County). 
According to the Department of Public Health’s Community Health Profiles, 40.7 percent 
of SPA 6 residents live in food-insecure households, and 43.4 percent of adults live in 
nutrition-insecure households, the highest rates of any SPA. 1 Only 56.6 percent of 
children in SPA 6 have good or excellent access to fresh fruits and vegetables, also the 
lowest rate in the County, and nearly one in three residents does not live near a 
supermarket or grocery store.2 
These inequities have direct health consequences. SPA 6 has the highest rate of 
diagnosed diabetes in the County, with 16.7 percent of adults affected.3 Diet-related 
illnesses such as diabetes and hypertension drive preventable hospitalizations, 
amputations, and early deaths, disproportionately affecting communities in South Los 
Angeles. 
 
1 Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, Community Health Profiles, Service Planning Area 6 
(data from the 2023 Los Angeles County Health Survey), https://ph-lacounty.hub.arcgis.com/pages/chp 
2 Ibid. 1 
3 Ibid. 1 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 17, 2026  
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
Farmers’ markets play a critical role in expanding access to healthy, affordable 
food. Since 2017, with a brief interruption during the COVID-19 pandemic, Sustainable 
Economic Enterprises of Los Angeles (SEE-LA), doing business as Food Access LA, has 
operated the Watts Willowbrook Farmers’ Market at the Martin Luther King, Jr. (MLK) 
Medical Campus. The market brings fresh produce directly to patients, staff, and 
surrounding Willowbrook residents and accepts CalFresh and WIC, helping reduce cost 
barriers for low-income households. 
The passage of H.R. 1 in July 2025 heightened the urgency of this work. The law 
enacted the largest reduction in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program funding in 
history, cutting an estimated $187 billion over ten years.4 As families lose food benefits, 
farmers’ markets that accept CalFresh experience reduced customer participation, and 
the small farmers who supply them face income losses. At the same time, Market Match, 
California’s program that doubles CalFresh dollars spent on fresh produce at farmers’ 
markets, received only one-time funding for Fiscal Year 2026-27, below sustainable levels, 
and federal matching funds have been withheld.5  
Despite these challenges, the Watts Willowbrook Farmers’ Market’s role in the 
community has only grown. Beyond offering fresh, seasonal produce, the market serves 
as a hub where community-based organizations share resources and hosts free nutrition 
classes and special programming in partnership with the MLK Outpatient Center. It also 
serves as a trusted community third space where neighbors gather, connect, and access 
resources such as health screenings, tree giveaways, and other services that meet 
residents where they are. The Department of Health Services has affirmed the market’s 
value as a direct link between medical care and healthy eating, and as a tool to help 
reduce diet-related disease. 
 
4 Congressional Research Service, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Related 
Nutrition Programs in P.L. 119-21: An Overview, R48552 (citing Congressional Budget Office estimates), 
July 23, 2025, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R48552/R48552.7.pdf 
5 “Market Match program secures $15 million in funding,” Gazetteer SF, July 2, 2026, 
https://sf.gazetteer.co/market-match-program-secures-15-million-in-funding; Ecology Center, “Farmers’ 
Markets Remain a Lifeline During the Federal Shutdown,” 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 17, 2026  
Page 3 
 
 
 
 
In March 2026, the Board of Supervisors approved the motion, “Fiscal Stewardship 
and Equitable Access in County Fee Waivers,” 6 directing the Chief Executive Officer to 
develop a Countywide Fee Waiver Policy that prioritizes events with the greatest equity 
impact, with final recommendations expected by the end of 2026. The Watts Willowbrook 
Farmers’ Market reflects these priorities: it is free and open to the public, accepts 
CalFresh and WIC, and serves a community with the County’s highest rates of food 
insecurity and diabetes. However, the market cannot wait for the policy to be finalized. 
Without a renewed license agreement, the community risks losing a vital source of fresh, 
affordable produce at a time when families are already facing reductions in food 
assistance. 
I THEREFORE MOVE THAT THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS: 
1. Find that the proposed granting of a non-exclusive, gratis license agreement to 
Sustainable Economic Enterprises of Los Angeles (SEE-LA) for the operation of a 
farmers market on Los Angeles County (County)-owned property is categorically 
exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to Section 15304(e) 
– Minor Alterations to Land and Class Four (4) of the County's Environmental 
Document Reporting Procedures and Guidelines. 
2. Find, pursuant to Government Code section 26227, that the portion of the County’s 
Martin Luther King Jr. Medical Campus proposed for the farmers market is not 
currently needed for exclusive County purposes during the specified Wednesdays 
and hours of market operation, which will be defined in the market license 
agreement. 
3. Find that the services to be provided by SEE-LA are necessary to meet the social 
needs of County residents and serve a public purpose by increasing access to 
fresh, affordable food in a community with the County’s highest rates of food 
insecurity and diabetes. 
4. Direct the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), or his designee, in consultation with the 
Director of the Department of Health Services (DHS), to waive the day-use permit 
 
6 https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/214035.pdf 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 17, 2026  
Page 4 
 
 
 
 
fee of $200 per market day for the duration of the market’s license term, not to 
exceed 55 market days per year. 
5. Delegate authority to the CEO, or his designee, in coordination with the Director of 
DHS, to negotiate, execute, and issue a gratis license agreement to SEE-LA within 
60 days, for a two-year term, for the operation of a farmers' market at the County-
owned Martin Luther King Jr. Medical Campus. 
6. Authorize the CEO, or his designee, to execute ancillary documentation approved 
as to form by County Counsel, and to take any other actions necessary and 
appropriate to implement and effectuate the market license. 
 
#  #  # 
(EA/YV/JY)

motions.title: SD2: Protecting Residents Facing H.R. 1 Work Requirements.
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Public Social Services and the Department of Human Resources to assess volunteer and paid employment opportunities, remove unnecessary background checks for non-sensitive volunteer positions, and report back in 14 days. It also directs DPSS to apply work requirements in the least restrictive manner permitted by law.
motions.backup_text:
- 
MORE - 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 
__________________________ 
 
BARGER 
__________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
__________________________ 
AGN. NO. 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL  
 
           November 10, 2026 
Protecting Residents Facing H.R. 1 Work Requirements 
On July 4, 2025, H.R. 1 was signed into law, imposing new work requirements on 
Medicaid (known as Medi-Cal in California) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance 
Program (SNAP, known as CalFresh in California). As of June 1, 2026, CalFresh 
recipients ages 18 through 64 who do not qualify for an exemption must complete 80 
hours per month of work, volunteering, or job training to maintain their benefits. For 
workfare assignments, required hours depend on the household’s CalFresh allotment 
divided by the minimum wage. Beginning January 1, 2027, adults ages 19 through 64 
enrolled in Medi-Cal through the Affordable Care Act expansion must work, volunteer, or 
attend school for at least 80 hours a month, or have monthly income of at least $580 to 
retain their health coverage, unless they qualify for an exemption, such as being the 
parent of a child 13 or younger.1 
Although the Medi-Cal work requirements do not take effect until January 1, 2027, 
Los Angeles County (County) has already seen significant caseload declines since H.R. 
1 was enacted. Between July 2025 and September 2026, the County lost roughly 393,000 
full-scope Medi-Cal enrollees, an 11.3 percent decrease, and approximately 140,000 
 
1 DHCS, “Medi-Cal Changes,” dhcs.ca.gov/medi-cal/updates/medi-cal-changes. 
 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
residents lost their CalFresh benefits.2 The Department of Public Social Services (DPSS) 
estimates that more than 280,000 CalFresh participants and 1.3 million Medi-Cal 
enrollees in the County will be subject to the new work requirements,3 and the Legislative 
Analyst’s Office projects that between 333,300 and 666,600 Medi-Cal beneficiaries are 
at risk of losing their health coverage through 2029-2030.4  
Loss of Medi-Cal coverage reduces revenue for clinics and hospitals and increases 
emergency room usage as residents lose access to non-emergency health care. Loss of 
CalFresh benefits increases food insecurity and places additional strain on food banks. 
These impacts affect every community in the County. Children represent nearly 20 
percent of those losing full-scope Medi-Cal and 44 percent of those losing CalFresh.5 
Many adults at risk of losing benefits are working or seeking work but cannot find enough 
consistent hours to meet the new thresholds. 
For residents without sufficient paid work, volunteering and workfare assignments  
are among the few remaining pathways to keep their benefits, but only if enough 
opportunities exist. Today, the supply of volunteer and workfare opportunities falls far 
short of need. As of October 2026, the County’s Workfare/Community Service 
Recruitment Hub, operated by Community Partners via County contract in partnership 
with DPSS, had interest from 75 organizations offering roughly 2,100 to 2,200 volunteer 
slots. However, many of these organizations have not completed the DPSS onboarding 
process to become official workfare sites. The Department of Economic Opportunity has 
found that the County’s existing workforce system, which currently serves more than 
100,000 jobseekers annually, is unlikely to absorb the volume of residents now needing 
 
2 Los Angeles County Department of Public Social Services, Statistical Analysis Reports from July 2025 – 
September 2026, DPSSAt-A-Glance 
3 Los Angeles County Department of Economic Opportunity, Public Workforce Support for HR1, updated 
September 24, 2026, p. 1 
4 Legislative Analyst’s Office, Key Impacts of H.R.1 on Medi-Cal and CalFresh from February 11, 2026 
5 Los Angeles County Department of Public Social Services, Statistical Analysis Reports from July 2025 – 
September 2026, DPSSAt-A-Glance 
 
 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
 
 
work or volunteer hours. The Board of Supervisors has already called on local businesses, 
nonprofits, faith organizations, and schools to step up, and directed County departments 
to identify and expand volunteer and workfare opportunities.6  
The County must strengthen its volunteer infrastructure to support residents in 
meeting the new requirements while also enhancing the public services volunteers help 
deliver.  Since 1981, the County’s Volunteer Program has successfully engaged tens of 
thousands of community members in meaningful volunteer work each year, ranging from 
elections support to animal care. This long-standing program demonstrates the 
community’s willingness to help support public sector services. However, many 
departments face challenges onboarding new volunteers, particularly when they are 
unfamiliar with the County’s Volunteer Program and related recruitment and screening 
processes.   
Under the Department of Human Resources (DHR) Policies, Procedures, and 
Guidelines No. 514 (PPG 514), background checks (Live Scan) are only required for 
positions designated as sensitive. Volunteers in non-sensitive roles, such as landscaping 
and waste removal, or those serving fewer than three days per event, are exempt. Despite 
this, many County departments still require a Live Scan background check for every 
volunteer, regardless of duties. This practice is costly, time-consuming, and unnecessarily 
excludes residents from opportunities like park and beach cleanups.  
With Medi-Cal work requirements taking effect on January 1, 2027, the County 
must act now and lead by example by creating an enhanced volunteer pipeline so that 
interested residents can learn about and access available volunteer opportunities.    
Unnecessary, burdensome, and expensive background checks should be eliminated to 
allow more residents to keep their Medi-Cal and CalFresh benefits, consistent with the 
County’s Fair Chance commitments. Departments should require background checks 
only for sensitive positions, in alignment with the County’s Fair Chance Ordinance and 
internal Fair Chance Policy. 
 
6 https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/206094.pdf 
https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/208808.pdf 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 4 
 
 
 
 
A thoughtful, coordinated approach is needed to identify, create, and promote 
appropriate volunteer opportunities that enable Medi-Cal recipients to quickly engage with 
County departments and programs. This includes streamlining existing departmental 
volunteer outreach and onboarding practices, and fully utilizing the consolidated volunteer 
opportunities platform supported by DHR. By proactively expanding non-sensitive 
volunteer roles, the County can continue to build a system that is efficient, fair, and 
welcoming. This will allow the County to help Medi-Cal and CalFresh recipients meet work 
and volunteer requirements while strengthening essential public services. 
Better data will be needed to understand who is at risk and whether the County 
interventions are effective. While DPSS has reported 28 County workfare sites, it lacks a 
geographic breakdown and clear information on available volunteer opportunities at each 
site. This information is particularly important because DPSS plans to launch the Work 
Requirement Application System in mid-2027 to help residents find volunteer and 
workfare sites. This online platform will allow organizations to submit work hours directly 
to DPSS, so that residents get credit for completed work.   
At the same time, residents need pathways not only to volunteering but also to 
paid employment and training. The County already offers a pipeline into County service 
through Preparing Los Angeles for County Employment (PLACE). The implementation of 
H.R. 1 creates an opportunity to expand these pathways through PLACE, partnerships 
with businesses and nonprofits, and the broader workforce system. Additionally, County 
policies, including Board Policy 9.120, Employment of Qualified GAIN/START 
Participants, directs departments to provide priority consideration to qualified participants 
in County workforce development programs when filling clerical and administrative 
positions. Strengthening these pathways will help residents maintain benefits while 
advancing toward stable, meaningful employment. 
I THEREFORE MOVE THAT THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:  
1. Direct the Director of the Department of Public Social Services (DPSS) to report 
back to the Board in writing in 14 days with: 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 5 
 
 
 
 
a. An assessment of the current volunteer opportunities that meet CalFresh and 
Medi-Cal work requirements for County residents.  Those opportunities should 
be broken down by County and non-County positions, geographic location 
(Service Planning Area and Supervisorial District), the potential number of total 
volunteer hours available per month at each site, and the type of work and skills 
required, if known; and 
b. An updated estimate of CalFresh and Medi-Cal recipients who must meet work 
requirements, disaggregated by Service Planning Area and Supervisorial 
District.  
2. Direct the Director of the Department of Human Resources (DHR) to: 
a. Work with departments to review volunteer positions currently designated as 
sensitive; provide guidance assessing whether those positions meet the criteria 
for sensitive positions under Policies, Procedures, and Guidelines 514 (PPG 
514); and require the removal of unnecessary background checks where 
appropriate. Departments should also be advised to develop and modify 
volunteer roles by limiting assigned duties to non-sensitive tasks that do not 
require Live Scan under PPG 514, and to clarify that the supervised use of 
County supplies, such as office materials or outdoor equipment, does not 
classify a role as sensitive; 
b. Develop a standard volunteer role template for positions not subject to Live 
Scan that departments can adopt; and 
c. Report back to the Board in writing in 14 days with a breakdown of the current 
volunteer positions that do not meet PPG 514, including a description each of 
role and its geographic location by Service Planning Area and Supervisorial 
District. 
3. Direct the Directors of the Department of Economic Opportunity and DHR to report 
back on current paid employment opportunities within the County connected to the 
PLACE program and other County employment pathways, for residents subject to 
work requirements, including which positions require Live Scan.  

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 6 
 
 
 
 
4. Direct the Director of DPSS to continue applying CalFresh and Medi-Cal work 
requirements in the least restrictive manner permitted by law. This includes 
screening all participants for exemptions, including physical or mental unfitness, 
before any discontinuance, and accepting self-attestation and third-party 
verification where permitted.  
5. Direct the Directors of DPSS and DHR to verbally present to the Board on 
November 17th on the above directives. 
#  #  # 
(EA/MR/YV/WG/CT)

motions.title: SD3: Exploring Housing Strategies and Expanded Supports for Transition-Age Youth (TAY)
motions.summary: Directs multiple County departments to report back on housing strategies, program expansions, and navigation supports for transition-age foster youth experiencing or at risk of homelessness. It also establishes a "Fast Pass" prioritization pilot and seeks ongoing funding to launch the "My Life, My Way" demonstration project.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
 
MITCHELL 
  _________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
  _________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 _________________________ 
 
BARGER 
 _________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
  _________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH                        November 17, 2026 
 
Exploring Housing Strategies and Expanded Supports for Transition-Age Youth 
(TAY)  
The 2026 Point in Time Homeless Count (Count) found that there were 3,658 
homeless youth in the Los Angeles Continuum of Care, 1,875 of whom were living on the 
street and 1,783 who were sheltered. Of these 3,658 young people, 2,786 identified as 
Transition-Age youth (TAY), between the ages of 18-24.1 While the statistics released 
this year did not contain information specifically on how many of these 3,658 youth had 
foster care involvement, it has been well established that many unhoused young people 
have child welfare experience. A January 20, 2026 report from the Department of Children 
and Family Services (DCFS) estimated that 1,245 TAY will age out of foster care in 2026, 
and a 2024 California Policy Lab report found nearly 1 in 4 youth formerly in foster care 
report having been homeless at some point between the ages of 21 and 23. This is 
unacceptable.2 
 
1 https://www.lahsa.org/documents?id=10078-yc26-coc-data-summary 
 
2 https://capolicylab.org/aging-out-of-foster-care-in-los-angeles/ 
 

2 
 
This Board of Supervisors (Board) has continually recognized the need to better 
support our young people as they exit foster care and reduce the risk that they experience 
homelessness following their transition from care. We have called on our County 
departments to align resources, share information, and explore innovative solutions, like 
a centralized hub, to better serve our young people with current and former foster care 
involvement. We have passed several motions over the last eighteen months on this very 
topic, pushing our County departments to take real, concrete actions to better support our 
young people. And we have continued to listen to our young people and advocates, who 
have shared their experiences, challenges, and ideas that should inform the County’s 
solutions and supports.  
The County has committed to better serving these young people.  The County’s 
new Department of Homeless Services and Housing (HSH), which launched in January 
2026, has staff dedicated to supporting transition-age youth and is actively pursuing 
funding to support housing and case management services for youth. In the FY 25-26 
Measure A Spending Plan, this Board responded to the needs of young people and 
allocated funding to keep certain TAY-facing services afloat. DCFS created the 
Supportive Housing Division in 2021, which focused on providing specialized housing 
support for foster youth in and exiting care. DCFS also recently mobilized an all hands-
on-deck effort in partnership with HSH to leverage expanded housing voucher 
opportunities from the federal government. The County’s Department of Mental Health 
(DMH) recently launched an Office of Transition Age Youth, which provides specialized 
services for transition-age youth, including emergency housing and independent living. 
The Justice, Care, and Opportunities Department (JCOD) has resources, including 

3 
 
housing supports, available for young people over the age of 18 with justice involvement, 
but it is unclear whether other County departments are aware of how to access these 
supports for the youth they serve. The Department of Youth Development (DYD) has also 
engaged in this space, proposing the launch of a new demonstration project, the “My Life, 
My Way Program,” focused on standing up a low-barrier support system for former foster 
youth who are no longer served by DCFS. DYD has emerged as a willing and active 
partner as we explore which department should ultimately lead care coordination for 
former foster youth.   
The extensive reports back from prior motions identified continued challenges, 
innovative recommendations, and concrete action steps.  These reports identified 
opportunities to strengthen transitional and permanent housing resources for youth who 
have recently aged out of foster care up to age 26, including capacity considerations 
and programs that could be strengthened with additional resources. Thanks to the work 
of the many County departments, advocates, and young people who contributed to 
those reports, this Board is prepared to act. We must further build out the continuum of 
services available to young people with experience in the foster youth system and those 
who have exited care, with the goal of reducing the likelihood that they spend even one 
night unhoused. We must increase program capacity where it is most needed, explore 
new solutions, rethink funding streams and expand our homeless prevention services 
for young people. Now is the time to strengthen our youth housing system and think big 
about what we can do to ensure our young people get the safe and secure housing they 
need and deserve. This Board’s expectation is that County departments will work harder 
than ever, in partnership with young people and advocates, to make demonstrable 

4 
 
progress in decreasing the number of homeless youth in the Los Angeles Continuum of 
Care.    
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Department of 
Children and Family Services (DCFS) to report back in writing in 60 days as follows: 
1. Explore the feasibility of expanding Project HopeBridge or a similar model beyond 
Service Planning Area (SPA) 6, with a plan for a phased implementation to the 
SPA with the next highest number of unhoused Transition-Age Youth (TAY). This 
should include a discussion of possible funding sources, including the Los Angeles 
County Development Authority’s (LACDA) Permanent Local Housing Allocation 
(PLHA) funding, any capacity needs, and a realistic timeline to offer this successful 
program to additional young people. This report should also include feedback from 
young people, including their insights into what makes the model appealing.  
2. In collaboration with the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Internal Services 
Department (ISD), and County Counsel, explore how to right-size the Transitional 
Housing Program-Plus (THP+) option for former foster youth, including those who 
are pregnant and parenting. This should include an examination of the number of 
beds actually needed in this program and a revision of the contracting process and 
contracts to the extent legally permissible and in line with state requirements to 
increase flexibility and accessibility for providers. Should the Department identify 
the need for additional THP+ beds, DCFS should work with the CEO to identify 
funding sources and work with the provider community to identify existing and new 
providers. The revised contracting process should identify opportunities to 
increase flexibility and accessibility for providers and reduce the timeline it takes 

5 
 
to execute a contract consistent with applicable legal requirements. DCFS should 
consult with the CEO and ISD, as well as integrate existing feedback from 
providers and from various crosswalk exercises into this process, to reexamine 
which requirements go above and beyond what is required by the state and 
whether modifications are appropriate. The report back to the Board must include 
their findings, planned next steps, and timeline for implementation.   
I, FURTHER MOVE, that the Board of Supervisors direct the Office of Child, Youth, 
and Family Well-Being (OCYFW) to report back in writing in 60 days as follows: 
3. In collaboration with the Chief Information Office (CIO), Chief Executive Office-
Policy Alignment Branch (CEO-PIAB), County Counsel and the Departments of 
Mental Health (DMH), DCFS, Homeless Services and Housing (HSH), Parks and 
Recreation (Parks), Public Health (DPH), Economic Opportunity (DEO), and Youth 
Development (DYD)  with a plan to develop and implement a pilot creating a “Fast 
Pass” prioritization process to prioritize navigation support for foster youth through 
age 26 who are at risk of or are experiencing homelessness, particularly those 
pregnant and/or parenting, for County administered and/or funded services and 
supports, where legally and regulatorily permissible. This pilot should focus on the 
programs funded and/or administered by DMH, DPH, HSH, DYD, DEO, and Parks. 
Once the report back has been submitted, the pilot should be implemented.  
a. The pilot implementation strategy should include a focus on: 
i. Establishing and/or strengthening cross-systems navigation and 
referral processes, including establishing clear points of contact and 
strengthening “warm handoff” practices to support continuity of care. 

6 
 
This should also include building feedback loops with young people 
and being responsive to youth needs, such as after-hours supports.  
1. This may include community-based care coordination models 
similar to those already implemented by DYD.  
2. This should also include setting expectations around referral 
times and include a mechanism for self-referral for young 
people who may not currently be connected to a system. 
ii. Developing trauma-informed methods to identify youth and young 
people not directly referred by a department. This should include 
establishing a secure verification process with DCFS to confirm 
current/former foster youth status, where necessary, without 
stigmatizing the young person.  
iii. Leveraging existing County data-sharing initiatives, such as the 
Community Information Exchange, the Countywide Information Hub, 
and consent-based data sharing tools to advance Fast Pass 
implementation goals, including consistent identification across 
systems. This should include coordinating with HSH to ensure 
alignment with ongoing youth homelessness system work to avoid 
creating a parallel pathway disconnected from existing homeless 
services infrastructure.  
iv. Strategies and metrics to track pilot outcomes, including referral 
times, youth experience, services needed and whether the pilot 
helps young people secure supports faster.  

7 
 
b. Before implementing a Fast Pass process for any specific program attached 
to a particular funding stream, law, or regulation, departments should work 
with County Counsel to ensure that doing so is legally permissible.  
4. In partnership with HSH, DCFS, DMH, the Department of Public Social Services 
(DPSS), LACDA, and the Justice, Care, and Opportunities Department (JCOD), 
complete a mapping of the Transition-Age Youth (TAY) Housing Continuum of 
Care. This report should include a discussion of system-wide resources, eligibility 
requirements, referral access, entry points, opportunities for case conferencing, 
funding streams attached to each particular resource, and how County 
departments could be better connecting and aligning efforts to support TAY. This 
work should include the perspective of the community-based organizations that do 
this work.  
I, FURTHER MOVE, that the Board of Supervisors direct the following 
Departments to report back as follows: 
5. CEO-Policy Implementation Branch (PIAB) and CIO to report back in 30 days on 
the status of their work to improve data sharing and support care coordination while 
ensuring that individuals maintain control over their information. The report should 
include updates and implementation timelines for the following and identification 
of any barriers: 
a. Strengthening consent-based information sharing; 
b. Standardizing authorization forms that allow youth and young adults to 
consent to the sharing of health and social services information across 
participating departments and providers; 

8 
 
c. Plan for continuing to support young people who chose not to consent to 
data sharing;  
d. The development of an electronic consent management system that will 
clarify what information can be shared, with whom, and under what 
conditions; and 
e. Integration of referral-tracking mechanisms. 
6. The Department of Homeless Services and Housing (HSH) to work with the Los 
Angeles County Affordable Housing Solutions Agency (LACAHSA) to explore how 
to align services, resources and supports for TAY, and report back in writing in 30 
days on those efforts.  
7. The Department of Public Social Services (DPSS) to report back in 60 days on the 
following:  
a. Estimated cost of implementing a “fast pass” system through any of the 
DPSS access points;  
b. The feasibility of having Linkages GAIN Social Workers (LGSWs), or 
another appropriate County classification, connect former foster youth or 
youth exiting foster care to DPSS services. If this is determined to not be 
feasible, identify alternative strategies for connecting former youth to DPSS 
services; 
c. Opportunities for DPSS to enhance its role in helping former foster youth 
access benefits and services, including expanding trauma-informed and 
cross-system training for staff; strengthening partnerships with community-
based organizations; improving coordination with housing and workforce 

9 
 
programs; and exploring enhancements to existing business processes to 
reduce procedural barriers. In this report, DPSS should include details 
about each of these opportunities and identify any potential barriers to 
implementation, including any associated funding needs; and 
d. Estimated costs of expanding the Springboard Guaranteed Income 
Program for General Relief TAYs, which supports housing needs, beyond 
their current 400 slots, in consultation with CEO-Poverty Alleviation 
Initiative. 
8. The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to report back in writing as a part of the FY 27-
28 recommended budget with sources of ongoing funding for the Department of 
Youth Development’s “My Life, My Way” program for three years in the amount of 
$2 million dollars annually for a total of $6 million beginning in the FY 27-28 budget.  
I, FURTHER MOVE, that the Board of Supervisors direct: 
9. The Department of Youth Development (DYD), in collaboration with HSH, to move 
forward with launching the “My Life, My Way Program” described in their May 18, 
2026 report back so that it can be implemented as soon as funding is identified. 
This 3-year demonstration project should be focused on young people ages 21-26 
who are former foster youth not receiving housing services from HSH and no 
longer connected to a social worker for case management support. This program 
should be designed to align with HSH’s TAY work to ensure that we are leveraging 
all available resources to support young people with foster care history.  
10. The Department of Mental Health (DMH) to report back in 60 days with the 
following: 

10 
 
a. A proposal to prioritize foster youth and recent former foster youth for 
Transitional Aged Youth (TAY) designated Interim Housing Program (IHP) 
beds, in consultation with DCFS. This proposal should include all legal 
and programmatic requirements and limitations, the proposed definition of 
former foster youth, best practices and trauma informed questioning about 
former foster youth status, how foster youth status would be collected, a 
timeline for implementation as soon as possible and the possibility of 
incorporating the data element into the DMH IHP system; 
b. How current and former foster youth in DMH’s housing program, including 
the Enhanced Emergency Shelter Program (EESP), are connected to the 
broader youth housing continuum of care; and 
c. A plan to coordinate among Full-Service Partnership (FSP) providers and 
Youth Access Center providers at the regional level to ensure facilitation of 
referrals to the FSP program, coordination of care and crisis response when 
services are medically necessary.  This report should also include a plan 
co-locate FSP at Youth Access Centers and to improve partnerships and 
services.

motions.title: SD3 - LA COUNTY 2028 GAMES CULTURAL PROGRAM FRAMEWORK
motions.summary: Adopts the LA County 2028 Cultural Program Framework, contingent on identifying funding, resources, and staffing. Directs the Department of Arts and Culture to launch the Creative Cities Network, develop an arts toolkit, pursue philanthropic partnerships, and coordinate cultural programming across departments for the 2028 Games.

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH 
November 10, 2026 
LA County 2028 Games Cultural Program Framework 
MOTION 
Mitchell 
_______________________________ 
Horvath 
_______________________________ 
Hahn 
_______________________________ 
Barger
