Solis 
_______________________________ 
The City of Los Angeles holds the bid for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games 
(Games) and the contract with the Los Angeles Organizing Committee (LA28), a private 
nonprofit entity that is the organizing committee for the 2028 Games. However, Olympic 
and Paralympic competitions will take place Countywide, requiring engagement from 
County operations as well as creating opportunities for our diverse communities, 
grantees, and partners. Furthermore, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) requires 
a Cultural Olympiad, providing a major opportunity to showcase the art and culture of the 
host city, region, and nation through diverse cultural programs and initiatives. 
In May 2026, LA28 unveiled its much anticipated Cultural Olympiad plan. The plan 
is guided by the goals of highlighting Los Angeles' story, collaborating with community 
partners, and igniting a culture of participation across six key art mediums: fashion, film, 
food, music, performance and visual art. LA28’s program will connect with cultural 
institutions, local artists, community organizations and neighborhood spaces where 
creativity already lives. LA28 will also provide arts organizations of all sizes with the 
opportunity to apply for the Official LA28 Cultural Olympiad Mark, ensuring that the 
creative institutions and grassroots groups defining the city's cultural landscape receive 

 
 
 
well-deserved recognition. Additionally, according to LA28, a dedicated Cultural Olympiad 
Calendar and Mapping platform is under development. This digital guide will map the 
region's cultural assets and showcase programming before transitioning to a trusted 
partner to maintain after the Games conclude. Both the City and the County are 
recognized as key partners in LA28’s plan. 
 
To prepare for supporting the local creative economy, the LA County Department 
of Arts and Culture contracted a consultant to host ten listening sessions and a community 
gathering. This initiative engaged 300 diverse stakeholders, including artists, municipal 
representatives, philanthropy, and cultural organizations, to shape the role of arts and 
culture in the 2028 Games. Building on the opportunities and recommendations identified 
in the report, the Department continues to collaborate with the City, LA28, and regional 
cultural networks to align and coordinate arts efforts across the region.  
 
Because of its role in regional leadership, services, infrastructure, and support, and 
the large-scale regional footprint of the Games, LA City, LA28 and other key partners 
recognize LA County as a key partner in supporting arts and culture for the 2028 Games. 
To that end, the Department has developed the “LA County 2028 Cultural Program 
Framework” which sets forth a countywide vision, goals, and programmatic strategies to 
support our region’s cultural sector and ensure communities across 88 cities and over 
120 Unincorporated Areas within the County have access to, and the benefits from, arts 
and culture in the Games and Cultural Olympiad. The Framework utilizes existing County 
and Department infrastructure and includes flexible programming proposals that can be 
activated when funding, partnerships, and resources become available. Further, the 
Framework has been developed to complement, and work in coordination and alignment 
with the City of LA’s 2028 Cultural Program for the Olympic and Paralympic Games 

 
 
 
Framework, LA28’s Cultural Olympiad Plan, and other cultural programs, while 
addressing gaps, needs, and opportunities in the region.  
 
The Framework will serve both as a guide for the Department’s activities and offer 
a unifying theme and programmatic pillars to support alignment, collaboration, and 
coordination in the region with pathways to participation for artists, cultural organizations, 
municipalities, funders, and local, state, national, and international partners, while 
remaining adaptable to evolve as partnerships, resources, and planning continue in the 
lead up to 2028. Ultimately, the County’s 2028 Cultural Program Framework proposes to 
showcase the vibrant arts and cultural sector and rich diversity of the County, embrace 
access and cultural participation, and most importantly, generate a legacy of a stronger 
cultural sector and creative economy, while sparking new collaborations and ways of 
working. Los Angeles County has recognized the value of arts, culture, and creativity as 
integral to civic life for all our people and communities. The Framework uplifts this vital 
role and the opportunity for access and legacy presented by 2028. 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors adopt the LA County 2028 
Cultural Program Framework with the understanding that implementation is contingent 
on identifying funding, resources, and staffing. 
I, FURTHER, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1. Direct the Center for Strategic Partnerships to collaborate with the Department of 
Arts and Culture, and any other relevant departments, to seek philanthropic 
partners for programs requiring additional funding in the 2028 Cultural Program 
Framework.   
2. Direct the Department of Arts and Culture, in collaboration with County 
Communications, to develop and promote the “Arts and Culture Toolkit for Cities 

 
 
 
and Unincorporated Areas”. 
3. Direct the Department of Arts and Culture to launch the “LA County Creative 
Cities Network” and invite representatives from the 88 cities, as well as staff from 
Board Offices in the County, to coordinate and support planning efforts related to 
arts and culture for the 2028 Games, at a minimum on a quarterly basis, 
effective, January 1, 2027. The Department should utilize existing convenings, 
such as the Municipal Arts Meeting, alongside virtual platforms to help partners 
stay informed, share updates, and identify opportunities for collaboration. 
4. Direct the Department of Arts and Culture to explore a collaboration with the City 
of Los Angeles on a 2028 Poster Competition that includes partnership with the 
cities of Paris and Brisbane. If feasible, the competition should actively engage a 
select group of Los Angeles-area colleges and art schools. Winning poster 
designs should be promoted and made accessible on digital and printed 
platforms. 
5. Direct the Department of Arts and Culture to convene regular working group 
meetings with department staff from Library, Parks & Recreation, Beaches & 
Harbors, the Los Angeles City/County Native American Indian Commission, and 
any other relevant departments, to collaborate and leverage existing resources 
that could generate cultural and artists opportunities in alignment with the 2028 
Cultural Program Framework. 
6. Direct County Departments, CEO Major Events, and Countywide 
Communications to collaborate with the Department of Arts and Culture where 
relevant, on programming, information, and promoting regional communications 
campaigns to constituents in support of the 2028 Cultural Program Framework.

Los Angeles County Department of Arts and Culture 
Cultural Program Framework: 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games 
 
 Vision Statement 
 
The Department of Arts and Culture (Department) envisions the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games (Games) and Cultural Olympiad as an 
opportunity to inspire, connect, engage, and strengthen communities through a dynamic cultural program that celebrates creative expression, 
champions arts and culture, uplifts LA’s cultural heritage, and reflects diverse voices of the LA County region in the global spirit of the Games, 
with lasting legacy benefits for arts, culture, and creativity as integral to civic life for all our communities beyond 2028. 
 Regional Alignment and Coordination 
 
The 2028 Cultural Program Framework sets forth a countywide vision, leveraging the Department’s distinct program assets, infrastructure, and 
reach to support our region’s cultural sector and ensure communities across 88 cities and over 120 Unincorporated Areas within LA County have 
access to, and the benefits from, arts and culture in the Games and Cultural Olympiad. It has been developed in close coordination with the host 
City of Los Angeles’ Department of Cultural Affairs (DCA); LA28, which is responsible for the official 2028 Cultural Olympiad; and many other key 
cultural stakeholders. It is intentionally designed to work in alignment with and in complement to City DCA’s 2028 Cultural Program for the  
Olympic and Paralympic Games, LA28’s Cultural Olympiad plans, as well as municipal cultural program plans, grantees, arts education partners, 
and other regional cultural initiatives, all of which have been engaged and mapped in the development of this framework. 
The Framework also seeks to maximize the County’s collective impact by incorporating programs and collaborations across County 
departments, such as Library, Parks & Recreation, Beaches & Harbors, Aging & Disability, Mental Health, Office of Child & Family Wellbeing, and 
County-owned cultural institutions Natural History Museums of LA County, Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), LA Plaza de Cultura y 
Artes, LA Philharmonic operating Hollywood Bowl and The Ford, Fairplex, and The Music Center. 
The Framework is intended to both guide the Department’s own activities, and to offer a regionally unifying thematic vision and set of programmatic 
pillars to support alignment, collaboration, and coordination across the region, with pathways to participation for artists, cultural organizations, 
municipalities, funders, and local, state, national, and international partners. It is intended to be adaptable, flexible, and built to evolve as 
partnerships, resources, and planning continue to develop in the lead up to 2028. 

 Goals 
 
1. 
Showcase the creative sector and the cultural diversity, heritage, artistry of the Los Angeles region, locally and on the global stage 
2. 
Engage diverse communities with wide arts access, programming, and cultural participation for local audiences, visitors, and viewers 
3. 
Spark new collaborations, ways of working, and exchange within the arts and across culture, sport, and education locally and globally 
4. 
Strengthen the cultural sector, support for the arts, cultural infrastructure, and creative economy of LA County 
5. 
Create a legacy beyond the Games with cross-sector benefits for the arts and for the civic life of our communities 
 Guiding Principles 
 
After the transformative 1984 Olympic Arts Festival, which brought art, performances, and cultural institutions to Los Angeles as a 
signature strategy, the unifying thematic vision of the 2028 Cultural Framework is to celebrate the rich tapestry of arts, culture, and creative 
communities of the Los Angeles region in the global spirit of the Games. Our guiding principles are to promote geographic and cultural equity 
through access to opportunities across LA County that reflect the cultural diversity of the region through an inclusive breadth of art forms and 
disciplines. We seek to offer resources that support the capacity of the local arts sector and use our role and this Framework to promote regional 
coordination, alignment, and collaboration. We recognize and support the foundational role of arts, culture, and creativity in civic life, building 
vibrant, healthy, sustainable, and resilient communities, and our human, community, and economic development. This Framework incorporates a 
belonging strategy which embraces communities’ need to feel seen, supported, connected, and proud for belonging to take hold, all of which are 
woven throughout the programmatic strategies, Department role, and activities described below. 
 Preparation and Planning 
 
The Department has convened over 300 cultural organization and arts field leaders, connected with global cities from prior Cultural 
Olympiads including a landmark Los Angeles x Paris Cultural Olympiad Leadership Exchange with artistic collaboration projects, and continues 
to engage with host DCA, LA28, municipal local arts agencies within the County, arts philanthropy, cultural organizations, and regional 
stakeholders to learn and shape how arts and culture are integrated into the 2028 Games. 
Key Takeaways: 
 
• 
Who the Games should serve: From the Report on Arts and Cultural Convenings for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, 
stakeholders overwhelmingly prioritized local residents (70%) over international visitors (30%) as the primary audience for arts and 
culture programming; with additional consideration for viewers online and broadcast 
• 
How to engage residents: Top program strategies include site-specific art installations and performances in public spaces, 
community-based festivals, and cross-cultural collaborations between local and international artists 
• 
What inclusion requires: Direct funding to community-based organizations beyond existing funds in 2026 and 2027, neighborhood- 

specific cultural hubs, marketing/visibility, and clear pathways to participation — with special attention to disability inclusion, Native 
cultures, and sustainability, and addressing barriers like geography, funding needs, and accessibility 
• 
How to build lasting legacy: Strong centralized leadership, strengthened infrastructure within the arts and across sectors, public 
art and programs that continue after the Games, and investment in the next generation through creative career pathways 
• 
2028 legacy themes for plans and programs: Disability access and inclusion, climate and environmental sustainability, 
health and wellbeing, youth development, economic opportunity, and LA’s cultural diversity 
 
 Our Role 
 
As the County’s local arts agency, the Department supports arts, culture, and creativity throughout the region as a funder, convener, 
partner, program lead, policymaker, and connector in the arts sector, across sectors, and to the vast reach of the County’s departments. For 
2028, the Department will leverage its role to support the arts field in five key ways in the phases before, during, and after the Games. 
• 
Readiness and Field Building: support readiness, capacity building, regional alignment, coordination, and collaboration through 
networks, convening, information sharing, professional development, and technical assistance 
• 
Resources, Funding, and Support: direct resources, funding, and support to artists, organizations, and partners to ensure sector 
capacity to deliver accessible programs, engage audiences, and participate in Games-related cultural festivals and initiatives 
• 
Maximize County Collaboration: engage the County’s departments and County cultural institutions to leverage assets, build 
cross-sector collaborations, cross-promote programming, and extend outreach to constituencies and communities countywide 
• 
Marketing, Communications, and Visibility: participate in regional marketing, promotion, and storytelling to amplify visibility, 
expand access to the arts, spotlight artists, events, and grantees, and drive audiences to partner platforms and event calendars 
• 
Legacy Beyond 2028: contribute to and carry forward positive outcomes for our arts sector and communities beyond the 
Games including lessons learned, stronger field networks, new partnerships, programs, art, and cultural infrastructure 
These will maximize the Department’s regional leadership role, reach, and infrastructure, address key needs and gaps, and work in tandem 
with LA28, DCA, philanthropy, County departments, and the wider arts field. 
 Our Strategies 
 
From our learnings, convenings, strategy development, and mapping of goals and program assets, resources, and opportunities 
within the Department, across the County portfolio, municipal local arts agencies, Games plans, and the culture field, several aligned 
program strategies emerged which are consolidated into four programmatic pillars that define our Cultural Program Framework: 
• 
Pillar 1: Arts and Culture for All - Public Programs, Exhibits, Live Arts, Events 
• 
Pillar 2: Year of Creative Youth - Arts Education, Youth Development, Creative Career Pathways 
• 
Pillar 3: Culture in Place - Civic Art, Cultural Hubs, Creative Placemaking and Keeping 

• 
Pillar 4: Arts All Access - Regional Marketing, Communications, Storytelling 
 
Each section below includes current planning underway utilizing existing programs, partnerships, capacity, and resources, followed by 
proposals that require new funding, staffing, and/or partnerships and may be activated only depending on available resources. 
 
 Pillar 1: Arts and Culture for All — Public Programs, Exhibits, Live Arts, Events 
 
 
2028 is an opportunity to expand access to the arts and LA’s cultural legacy through a rich array of cultural programs, exhibits, performing 
arts, festivals, and events across the LA region, enlivening joy, civic engagement, social connection, economic activity, cultural diversity and 
heritage. The Department will promote LA County programs and support arts and culture nonprofits to deliver robust, accessible programming for 
cultural participation of local communities and visitors in the lead up to and during the Games and Cultural Olympiad. 
 
Current Plans: 
 
Flexible Grants for Arts Organizations 
The Department will leverage its existing Organizational Grant Program (OGP) and Community Impact Arts Grants (CIAG) infrastructure, which 
together includes over 600 organizations, to connect grantees with Games and Cultural Olympiad information and opportunities. Existing grantees 
will be invited to incorporate Games themes into programming across all artistic disciplines, from visual arts and music to theater, film, and literary 
arts, and to optionally include 2028 activities in their application for grant support, within the County’s existing grants program budget allocation. 
 
County Programs and Collaborations 
The Department will engage County-owned cultural institutions and venues, and County departments, including those in the County 2028 Games 
working groups organized by CEO, to cross-promote and collaborate on arts and cultural programming. These departments include but are not 
limited to County Parks & Recreation, Library, Beaches & Harbors, Aging & Disabilities, and activations could include those departments’ wraps 
and library bookmarks, library “one book” programming, and free concerts in parks and other County sites. 
 
  Pillar 2: Year of Creative Youth — Arts Education, Youth Development, Creative Career Pathways 
 
 
2028 presents an opportunity to leverage the Games as a youth engagement platform, connecting young people to sports, arts, and education. To 
build a youth arts legacy for the 2028 Games, the Department will dedicate 2028 as a Year of Creative Youth. From summer/fall 2027 through 
summer 2028, young people across LA County will engage in arts, learning, and creativity — in schools, communities, civic spaces, and 
institutions — as a celebration of young talent, creative expression, cultural diversity, and the Games. Through access to arts, play, and creative 
storytelling, youth will build their voice, social-emotional wellbeing, civic pride, and career skills. 

Current Plans: 
 
Arts Internship Programs 
The Department will leverage its existing LA County Arts Internship Program (AIP) and Bloomberg Arts Internship (BAI) program in 2027-2028 
to connect college students and rising high school seniors with work-based learning and creative career exploration. The Department will 
invite arts and culture organizations hosting interns to incorporate Games and Cultural Olympiad themes into intern projects, with related 
cultural excursions, field trips, and career readiness activities. 
 
Creative Wellbeing Programming — Arts for Youth Mental Health 
During 2026-2028, the Department will expand Creative Wellbeing, with its community-based arts organization partners, to provide healing-
centered arts engagement for youth, including systems-impacted, foster and transition-age youth (TAY), LGBTQ+ youth, and the adults who care 
for them. Programming for 2028 will feature art making, performances, cultural traditions, curricula, and Games themes to foster community 
pride, healing, and wellbeing through the arts at locations such as parks, libraries, foster group homes, schools, County-affiliated Fan Zones, and 
special events. While budget resources are already in place for these activities, additional funds could expand frequency and reach of 
programming. Creative Wellbeing services will include County parks sites and other site partner locations in Unincorporated Areas. 
 
2028 Arts and Justice Youth Mural Legacy 
Through the Department’s partnerships with the Boyle Heights Arts Conservatory Mural Workforce Academy at Barry J. Nidorf Juvenile Hall and 
Homeboy Arts Academy, the Department will engage system-involved youth in mural projects building job-ready skills, creative confidence, and 
leadership. Completed murals would transform shared spaces and affirm young people as artists and storytellers, while highlighting Games 
themes and creating a legacy of youth justice and healing. Additional arts programs, such as music and writing, will engage youth in arts-based 
youth development across Probation camps and halls where aligned with the Framework and Games themes. 
 
2028 Arts Education Curriculum Toolkit 
The Department will collaborate with the Olympic Foundation for Culture and Heritage and local partners to create a special 2028 arts education 
curriculum guide as a resource for LA County school districts, arts education organizations, and libraries. The toolkit will utilize the Olympic 
Museum’s collections with opportunities for teaching artists, schools, organizations, and educators to engage youth and students and build 
connections between Los Angeles County and the Games — through arts, culture, and creativity. The curriculum guide will be shared with all school 
districts including those located in and serving Unincorporated Areas, as well as arts education organizations and the County library system 
countywide. As the first arts education curriculum guide created with the Olympic Foundation for the Games, it has potential for wide reach. 
 
Proposals: 
 
School District Arts Education — Expanded for 2028 

The Department seeks to increase Advancement Grant funding for school districts as a platform to engage K-12 students in arts education leveraging 
Games themes and resources — including special 2028 arts education curricula, district art shows, artist in-school residencies, field trips to cultural 
partners, special exhibits, and school arts events. This funding leverages the County’s reach, expands access to the arts, arts integration across 
subjects, and provides resources to support student engagement and arts education advancement, with priority for historically underserved 
communities. This proposal leverages the public-private Arts Ed Collective and furthers the LA County Regional Blueprint for Arts Education adopted 
by the Board of Supervisors and ensures that more of the County’s 1.2 million students across the region participate meaningfully in 2028 creativity. 
Advancement Grants are offered to eligible school districts located in and serving both municipalities and Unincorporated Areas of the County. 
LA County Arts Internship Program — Expanded for 2028 
The Department seeks funding to expand the LA County Arts Internship Program across one or more cycles (2027, 2028, and beyond) to bring the 
program back to a full 228 paid internships, engaging college students of diverse backgrounds in creative career pathways connected to the Games, 
with lasting benefit to both students and the arts organizations that host them. In a special 2028 program cycle, interns may have the opportunity to 
work on 2028 Cultural Olympiad and related projects with their internship hosts, providing critical support to the County’s arts organizations’ 
program delivery during the Games year, with paid work-based learning for youth across positions in marketing, production, events, and more. 
Program elements, such as peer group events, panel talks, and the annual Arts Summit Day, would feature creative careers across arts, sports, and 
entertainment, Games themes, and 2028 cross-sector topics such as climate and environmental sustainability and disability artistry. 
 
2028 Poster Competition 
The 2024 Cultural Olympiad Poster Competition, which the Department co-led with City of Paris Department of Cultural Affairs, along with additional 
partners DCA and Seine Saint Denis as part of the official 2024 Cultural Olympiad, brought together Paris and LA art schools for students to create 
original poster designs as part of in-class art instruction. Through the project, Otis College of Art and Design, ArtCenter Pasadena, and CalArts 
collaborated for the first time. Twenty-four winning designs were selected by international jury to amplify the bonds between the Paris 2024 and Los 
Angeles 2028 Games and were exhibited in Paris, County and City sites, and digitally. Building on the success of that program, the Department will 
explore opportunities to showcase the existing 2024/2028 poster designs for the 2028 Games and Cultural Olympiad, such as international 
hospitality houses, County and City sites, cultural diplomacy protocol, and as posters, cards, or digital artworks. The Department will also explore 
the feasibility of a new 2028 Poster Competition to further engage LA County colleges, college-level art schools, or K-12 students to create new 
original poster art designs highlighting creativity, arts learning, and creative careers for LA County youth in connection with LA’s visual identity and 
the global spirit of the Games. This can be explored as a collaboration between LA County/City and Brisbane for 2028/2032 to continue a legacy of 
cultural exchange and diplomacy through the arts. 
 
 Pillar 3: Culture in Place — Civic Art, Cultural Hubs, Creative Placemaking and Keeping 
 
 
Creative placemaking and keeping engages the transformative role of arts and culture to celebrate diverse cultures, support local creative 
economies, build social cohesion, and create vibrant spaces of creative activity, wellbeing, and belonging. The Department envisions the LA region 

as a canvas for art, design, creativity, and cultural stewardship. By stewarding the LA County Civic Art Collection, investing in artists as creative 
strategists, and embedding place-based cultural districts and hubs in Framework strategies, the Department connects communities to place, 
identity, history, design, and each other. With additional funding, these efforts expand further — animating Games and cultural hubs as platforms of 
community pride and artistic expression, and telling the story of Los Angeles through public art, civic space, and the people who call it home. 
 
Current Plans: 
 
Creative Strategist Artist-in-Residencies 
Artists and creative workers are creative strategists, bringing creative and arts-based approaches to improve civic life working alongside County 
departments in the Creative Strategist-Artist in Residence program. The Department will leverage Creative Strategist residencies to support 2028 
Games and cross-sector themes such as disability access and artistry, sustainability, public infrastructure, cultural diversity and preservation. 
 
Cross-Sector Arts — Health, Healing, and Creative Recovery 
The Department will continue its work at the intersection of arts, health, and creative recovery including the Arts and Health Summit, a project in the 
unincorporated County community of Florence-Firestone for the Vision Zero initiative to create safer streets, and the Library Cultural Climate  
Commons wildfire recovery project, supporting community artmaking, a digital archive, and cultural preservation in unincorporated Altadena. 
 
Proposals: 
 
First Peoples — "We Are Still Here" Visibility Initiative 
To amplify the story of LA as home to one of the nation's largest urban Native American populations, the Department would explore an 
awareness campaign. Strategies to call attention to the American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) community in Los Angeles County could 
include: "We Are Still Here — Welcome to Los Angeles," large-scale digital billboard(s) using the portrait photography commissioned for the 
“We Are Still Here.” Report on Past, Present, and Ongoing Harms Against Local Tribes; collaboration with the Los Angeles City/County 
Native American Indian Commission (LANAIC) to present the annual Native American Heritage Month art exhibit — which typically takes 
place in November — during the Games and Cultural Olympiad; outreach to Native artists and organizations for grants, civic art, and 
communications opportunities; and outreach for the Countywide Land Acknowledgment toolkit to encourage the County’s 88 municipalities 
to engage with local Tribes. 
 
Cultural Preservation — 1984 Games Civic Art Conservation 
The Department seeks to undertake a conservation project for a historically and culturally significant 19 84 Games’ mural artwork in the 
County Civic Art Collection, revitalizing, documenting, and engaging the living artist. This strategy will incorporate apprenticeships, provide 
creative career pathways, enhance civic spaces, steward cultural heritage, and create economic opportunities for local artists and conservators, 
while uplifting the role of art and murals in LA’s history hosting the Games, connecting 1984 to 2028 today.

Now more than a year and a half after the Eaton Fire swept through Altadena, the 
County has made great strides toward its recovery, including issuing more than 3,700 
building permits, with more than 220 homes completing construction. As momentum 
continues and we welcome more Altadenans home, it’s important that the local arts and 
culture are well represented in Altadena’s recovery.  
Altadena has long been home to a vibrant arts community. One of our County’s parks in 
Altadena is named after renowned local artist Charles White. Many artists have called 
Altadena home, including numerous who lost their houses and artwork in the fire. In the 
immediate aftermath of the fire, the Department of Arts and Culture hosted several 
conservation clinics in the community in partnership with professional conservators to 
clean and restore damaged artwork.  
In an effort to offer professional opportunities to Altadena artists, and to create a 
beautiful and welcoming atmosphere for residents as they move back home, the 
Departments of Arts and Culture and Public Works are partnering to launch the 
County’s first utility box artwork project in Altadena. Public Works has identified 10 utility 
box locations across Altadena where artwork will be most visible and equitably 
distributed among different parts of the community. Each box will feature artwork from a 
different local artist. The project is slated to cost $59,000 using the Fifth District’s civic 
art pooled funds.  
To ensure thoughtful and thorough engagement with local artists and the community at 
large, it’s important that the consultant stewarding this project be well integrated in 
Altadena and be known and trusted by residents and artists alike. Austin Scott is an 
artist and Altadena resident who has been actively and regularly creating art for the 
community since the fire. Since March 2025, he has completed nine murals, including 
the largest in Altadena: an 85-foot-long piece entitled “From Rails to Trails: Echo 
Mountain” along the Altadena Crest Trail. The project engaged more than 80 community 
volunteers, including several artists, to collaboratively complete the artwork.  
- - - MORE - - -

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR KATHRYN BARGER 
November 10, 2026 
Page 2 
 
Additionally, he’s recently worked on a 900-square-foot mural at George’s Corner Store, 
garnering participation from more than 100 community members of all ages. His mural 
“Dream Bigger” at Alma Fuerte Public School also included participation from more than 
a dozen local children. Further investing in local schools, Scott serves as the co-chair of 
the beautification committee at Altadena Arts Magnet and is working with numerous 
school districts across the region on collaborative mural work, where he is teaching 
students how to create murals of their own.  
 
Additionally, Scott has partnered with various local businesses, including 
Unincorporated Coffee Roasters, Altadena Cookie Co., Webster's Community 
Pharmacy, and Altadena Music Center on murals and illustrations that bring vibrancy to 
their workplaces. He’s also helped with branding for local businesses, created 
illustrations of homes lost in the fire, and done live caricature drawings at community 
events. Scott is currently planning his next collaborative piece, his largest yet, focused 
on Altadena's Black history. 
 
Scott is committed to engaging and including residents in the artistic process, believing 
strongly that the arts are an investment in residents’ healing and in the community itself. 
Given his collaborative spirit and deep relationships in the Altadena community, Scott’s 
involvement in the utility box artwork project, where he would create community 
engagement opportunities and identify and steward the work of 10 diverse artists, would 
create seamless continuity with the existing arts efforts underway in Altadena.  
 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Los Angeles County 
Department of Arts and Culture to enter into a Sole Source Agreement with Austin Scott 
in the amount of $59,000, using the Fifth District’s civic art pooled funds, to serve as the 
consultant responsible for community engagement, artist selection, contracting with the 
10 participating artists, and delivery of the utility box artwork project in Altadena, and 
authorize the Director of Arts and Culture to execute necessary contract amendments, 
including change orders, and to take all actions needed to deliver the project. 
 
 
#          #          #

motions.title: SD4: Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for Disability Services in Los Angeles County
motions.summary: Approves and adopts the Aging and Disabilities Department's Five-Year Strategic Plan for people with disabilities within existing resources. Directs the department to establish a Countywide Disability Services Hub, report on progress every 180 days, pursue external funding, and develop inclusive recruitment strategies.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
 
HAHN 
__________________________ 
 
BARGER 
__________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
__________________________ 
AGN. NO.__________             
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN 
November 10, 2026 
 
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified 
Vision for Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
California is changing.  As the number of older adults and people with disabilities 
grows, so does the state’s understanding that their full participation in community life is 
not optional but essential to California’s social and economic vitality.  This recognition 
shaped the California Master Plan for Aging (MPA), released in 2021, which laid out a 
10-year vision for an age and disability friendly California.  The plan makes a simple but 
powerful promise: that every Californian, regardless of age or ability, should be able to 
live with dignity, independence, and choice.  Achieving that promise requires strong 
disability services, accessible housing, transportation, home and community-based 
support, long term services and supports, health care, and caregiver assistance.  
Nowhere is this work more urgent than in Los Angeles County (County), home to 
one of the nation’s largest and most diverse disability communities.  The County’s 
population spans every age, background and experience, and its needs continue to 
evolve.  Recognizing this, the Aging and Disabilities Department (AD) set out to build a 
stronger, more coordinated system of support.  This effort began with a motion in August 
2020 that created the Department itself. 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
A key part of this evolving system, and one of AD’s newest developments, is the  
recent designation of Los Angeles County’s Aging and Disability Resource Connection 
(ADRC) network by the California Department of Aging (CDA). Designed as a trusted “No 
Wrong Door” entry point, the ADRC offers residents a network where older adults, people 
with disabilities, caregivers, and families can find guidance, person-centered counseling, 
and warm handoffs to the services they need.  In a county as large and complex as Los 
Angeles, the ADRC model is becoming an essential bridge, connecting people to the right 
long-term services and supports at the right moment and reducing the fragmentation that 
has long made service navigation difficult.  As AD strengthens its role as the Countywide 
administrator, the ADRC network provides the backbone for a more consistent, 
accessible, and coordinated system. 
California’s ADRCs are built on core partnerships between Independent Living 
Centers (ILCs) and Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs), along with a network of extended 
partner organizations. The heart of disability leadership in the County has always lived in 
the community, and that is where the ILCs shine. Long before the County had the 
opportunity to start building a unified system, ILCs were already doing the work: 
disability-led, community-rooted, and grounded in the principles of self-determination and 
peer support. While traditional service providers play an essential role in delivering direct 
supports across the continuum of care, ILCs bring something fundamentally different. 
They are places where people with disabilities can walk in and see themselves reflected 
in leadership, the staff, and the philosophy. ILCs offer what no other part of the system 
can replicate through peer counseling, skills training, housing navigation, advocacy, and 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
transition support shaped by lived experience. Their deep roots in the disability rights 
movement make them not just service providers, but cultural anchors and trusted 
advocates. 
In 2025, AD embarked on its most ambitious effort yet, a five-year strategic 
planning process designed to understand what people with disabilities across the County 
need most.  AD conducted a sweeping Countywide needs assessment through extensive 
stakeholder interviews, data reviews, best-practice research, and a deep collaboration 
with the County’s Commission on Disabilities. 
At the heart of this process was the public.  A Countywide survey was completed 
where experiences, frustrations, and hopes were shared.  These responses painted a 
vivid picture. Many struggled to navigate complex service systems or simply didn’t know 
where to turn for help.  Others feared losing services due to limited resources. Housing 
emerged as a major barrier; too little was accessible, and even less was affordable.  
Social isolation affected 40% of respondents. Public transit was often inaccessible. Many 
respondents also indicated that service providers require additional training and a more 
comprehensive understanding of disability. 
With this foundation, AD brought stakeholders together for a day-long visioning 
session to imagine the future of disability services in the County.  The message was clear; 
AD must lead by example.  Strengthening the department’s own internal policies and 
practices was not only a priority, but it was also the first step toward modeling accessibility, 
inclusion, and collaboration for the entire County. 
 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
From this collective work emerged four overarching goals: 
1. Strengthen Capacity and Infrastructure 
2. Increase Accessibility and Navigation 
3. Expand Advocacy and Education 
4. Enhance Services and Supports 
These goals form the backbone of the Disability Services Strategic Plan, each supported 
by objectives and performance indicators laid out in a five-year implementation roadmap.  
The plan is intentionally structured, with a staggered timeline that allows AD to focus on 
specific areas each year while maintaining momentum. It also emphasizes coordination 
at key transition points across the lifespan, from early childhood to school age, from youth 
to adulthood, and into older adulthood, reflecting the County’s commitment to supporting 
people with disabilities at every stage of life. 
The Strategic Plan does not change the statutory authority of other County 
departments.  Instead, it positions AD as the Countywide convener, coordinator, and 
standard-setter, and the hub that brings together the many resources scattered across 
County systems.  Given budget realities, the first phase focuses on identifying and 
aligning existing resources, maintaining continuity of existing Disability Services Branch 
functions, and building a stronger, more connected foundation. 
The Los Angeles County Disability Services Strategic Plan represents a shared 
vision, a future where people with disabilities of all ages can thrive in communities that 
are equitable, accessible, and responsive to their needs.  This narrative marks the 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
beginning of the policies, partnerships, and investments required to make that vision real 
for every resident of Los Angeles County. 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors approve and adopt the Los 
Angeles County’s Aging and Disabilities Department’s Five-Year Strategic Plan to 
address needs for people with disabilities, within existing fiscal resources, and with the 
following: 
1. Direct the Aging and Disabilities Department (AD), in collaboration with the Chief 
Executive Office (CEO), to provide written updates to the Board on progress toward 
completion of the objectives outlined in the Disability Services Strategic Plan within 
180 days and every 180 days thereafter, with the reporting requirement sunsetting in 
December 2028. The initial report should also include recommendations for the 
repurposing of existing positions, reclassification of existing positions, or creation of 
new classifications, if necessary, to support the AD Disability Services Hub, based on 
workload, service demand and performance metrics identified in the Strategic Plan, 
including positions focused on: 
• Countywide disability services coordination 
• Information and assistance / system navigation 
• Data, performance, and outcomes management 
• Accessibility and Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) advancement 
• Community and provider network engagement 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
This includes the identification of potential funding sources and cost neutral strategies. 
AD will provide a verbal presentation of the initial report back to the Family and Social 
Services Cluster, within 180 days of adoption of this motion; 
2. Direct AD to formally establish and operationalize a Countywide Disability Services 
Hub, anchored in the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) and No 
Wrong Door framework, to serve as the central coordinating entity for disability-related 
programs, policies, services, and cross-department initiatives across Los Angeles 
County;  
3. Recognize that disability-related services and resources currently exist across 
multiple Los Angeles County (County) departments and community-based agencies 
and that a centralized coordination structure is necessary to reduce fragmentation, 
improve navigation, and mitigate service access risks for County residents; 
4. Direct AD, in collaboration with the Chief Executive Office (CEO), to establish the 
governance structure, operational protocols, shared service navigation standards, 
data-sharing practices, and interdepartmental coordination mechanisms necessary to 
implement the AD Disability Services Hub and improve continuity of services across 
the lifespan; 
5. Authorize AD and their non-profit, the Community Services Resource Corporation to 
pursue and accept federal, State, philanthropic, and private funding opportunities to 
expand the capacity of the AD Disability Services Hub and strengthen the Countywide 
disability services network;  

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR JANICE HAHN  
Advancing Accessibility and Community Living: Aging and Disabilities Unified Vision for 
Disability Services in Los Angeles County 
November 10, 2026 
 
6. Direct AD, in partnership with Department of Human Resources (DHR), to develop 
inclusive recruitment strategies to further support the hiring and retention of individuals 
with disabilities and lived experience within AD. 
#          #          #

motions.title: SD2: Strengthening Increasing Access to Mobility for Youth and Families and Realizing Cost Savings Through Partnership with LA County Metropolitan Transportation Authority.
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Children and Family Services and Metro to assess youth receiving agency-funded transit passes and transition eligible individuals into Metro's GoPass and LIFE programs. Instructs them to identify replacement youth engagement incentives and report back within 60 days.
motions.backup_text:
- MORE - 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL 
___________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
___________________________ 
 
HAHN 
___________________________ 
 
BARGER 
___________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
___________________________ 
 
 
 
AGN. NO 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
 
Increasing Access to Mobility for Youth and Families and Realizing Cost Savings 
Through Partnership with LA County Metropolitan Transportation Authority  
 
Los Angeles County (County) Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) 
works hand-in-hand with youth and families across the County and provides essential 
safety-net services, including to foster youth, transition-age youth, parents, resource 
parents, relative caregivers, and guardians. As part of DCFS’s ongoing case 
management and monthly contact with youth and caregivers, Children’s Social Workers 
(CSW) assess and respond to a range of needs that support the safety, well-being, 
stability, and permanency of children and youth. Transportation is an important 
component of this work, helping youth and caregivers access required and supportive 
services, including family visitation, medical and behavioral health appointments, 
educational activities, court-related obligations, and other activities identified in a youth’s 
case plan or otherwise necessary to support family stability.   
Currently, DCFS purchases stored-value transit passes directly from the Los 
Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro) for eligible youth and 
caregivers who require public transportation assistance. These transit passes are 
provided through DCFS’s ongoing case management. In total, DCFS spends 
approximately $1.5 million annually on transit passes for youth and families. 
There is potential for DCFS to realize significant cost savings by partnering with 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
Metro to identify and enroll eligible youth and caregivers in Metro’s existing free-and-
reduced fare programs, including Metro’s GoPass and LIFE programs, rather than 
continuing to purchase stored-value passes on a monthly basis, 
Metro’s GoPass program offers up to 15 months of unlimited rides on Metro and 
18 partner transit agencies across the County for eligible students enrolled in participating 
K-12 schools, adult schools, and community colleges. Currently, 14 school districts, 
charter networks, and private schools participate in GoPass, including Los Angeles 
Unified School District, Pasadena Unified School District, Long Beach Unified School 
District, and Montebello Unified School District, among others, as well as Community 
College Districts in Los Angeles, Cerritos, Santa Monica, and more. Any DCFS-involved 
youth enrolled in a school district, community college, or school participating in GoPass 
is eligible to ride for free on Metro and its partner agencies.  
This raises the possibility that DCFS is currently double-paying for transit by 
purchasing stored-value Metro transit passes for youth who are already eligible for the 
GoPass program through their school. Metro can collaborate with DCFS to develop a 
process that allows CSW’s to facilitate the enrollment of eligible youth in GoPass during 
regularly scheduled meetings, while preserving DCFS-funded transportation assistance 
for individuals whose transportation needs are not met through GoPass.  
Metro’s LIFE Program provides 20 free rides every month on Metro and 16 other 
participating transit agencies across the County, plus 90 days of free rides upon signing 
up, for income-qualified riders. Residents in households under specified income limits, or 
those who receive benefits such as Electronic Benefit Transfer, Medi-Cal or 
Supplementary Security Income, or who participate in other qualifying programs, are 
eligible for LIFE. Enrolling guardians in LIFE would provide access to a greater number 
of rides than many currently receive through the existing stored-value cards, and would 
enroll them in an automatically recurring monthly benefit after the initial 90-day period of 
unlimited rides.  
This approach can reduce duplicative expenditures, increase awareness and 
utilization of existing public transportation benefits, and help ensure that youth and 
caregivers have reliable transportation to maintain connections with family, school, 
employment, health services, and other supports. 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
November 10, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
 
 
I THEREFORE MOVE THAT THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS: 
1. Direct the Interim Director of the Department of Children and Family Services 
(DCFS), in coordination with the Chief Executive Officer of the Los Angeles 
County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro), or their designee, to: 
a. Conduct an assessment of youth currently receiving agency-funded 
transit passes and identify opportunities to transition eligible individuals 
to Metro’s existing free-and reduced-fare programs, and partner with 
Metro to develop a system that enables DCFS to enroll eligible youth in 
the Metro GoPass program and caregivers in the Metro LIFE program. 
DCFS shall maintain an appropriate DCFS-funded transportation option 
for those who are not eligible for GoPass or LIFE, or whose 
transportation needs are not addressed by these programs; 
b. Identify and implement a replacement incentive to sustain monthly 
engagement by youth who no longer receive stored-value Metro transit 
passes as an incentive; and 
c. Report back to the Board in writing within 60 days with an 
implementation timeline, including key milestones developed in 
partnership with Metro, and proposed metrics to measure success over 
time, including a plan to track GoPass and LIFE enrollment among 
DCFS youth, caregivers, and guardians over time. 
 
#          #          # 
 
 
(CA/LH/MR)

motions.title: SD3 & SD1: Strengthening County Gender-Based Efforts, Services and Supports for Survivors of Intimate Partner Violence
motions.summary: Directs County departments to enhance intimate partner violence services, identify funding for legal assistance and a centralized survivor intake hotline, and evaluate emergency housing resources. It also authorizes a sole-source contract with Downtown Women’s Center for shelter referral consulting services.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
 
MITCHELL 
  _________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
  _________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 _________________________ 
 
BARGER 
 _________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
  _________________________ 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
    AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS LINDSEY P. HORVATH            November 10, 2026 
AND HILDA L. SOLIS                    
 
Strengthening County Gender-Based Efforts, Services and Supports for Survivors 
of Intimate Partner Violence  
Domestic violence (DV) or intimate partner violence (IPV), defined as any physical 
violence, sexual violence, stalking, or psychological aggression perpetrated by a family 
member or a current or former intimate partner, including spouses, boyfriends, girlfriends, 
ongoing sexual partners, and dating partners, continues to impact individuals and families 
throughout Los Angeles County. Nationally, more than 1 in 3 women experience sexual 
violence, physical violence, and/or stalking by an intimate partner during their lifetime; 
about 16 million women said that they first experienced intimate partner violence before 
the age of 181. According to the California Department of Justice, in 2023 Los Angeles 
County recorded 5.6 domestic violence-related calls for assistance per 1,000 adults aged 
18-692.  The 2023 Los Angeles County Health Survey indicates that 15.3% of women in 
Los Angeles over the age of 18 and 6.7% of men reported ever being physically or 
 
1 https://www.cdc.gov/intimate-partner-violence/about/index.html 
2 https://www.kidsdata.org/export/pdf?cat=3 

2 
 
sexually abused by an intimate partner3 and the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey reports 
that 7.8% of high school students in the Los Angeles Unified School District who had 
dated someone reported experiencing physical dating violence in the past year.4  
Data from the County’s Child Protection Hotline (Hotline) run by the Department of 
Children and Family Services (DCFS) speaks to the connection between IPV/DV and the 
child welfare system. 72% of DCFS investigations with IPV/DV concern a child under age 
5, with 38% of those involving children under the age of 1. 1 in 3 investigations involving 
IPV also included concerns of substance abuse and/or mental health concerns. This is 
true for children of any age. According to a 2021 report5, 51.6% of 38,618 open DCFS 
cases the previous year had past or current concerns of domestic violence identified by 
DCFS caseworkers. The trauma of domestic violence and potential family separation has 
significant health impacts for adult survivors and their children, and require specialized 
supports and resources.  
In the past year, there have been multiple domestic violence-related murder-
suicides in Los Angeles County involving intimate partners and children. Since March 
2026, at least six apparent murder-suicides have been reported in the Third District alone, 
collectively resulting in the deaths of at least 15 people, including four children. In 2024 
and 2025, at least 63 women were killed by someone suspected to be a current or former 
partner, family member, or partner of a family member, according to an LA Times analysis 
 
3 2023 Los Angeles County Health Survey; Office of Health Assessment and Epidemiology, Los Angeles 
County Department of Public Health. 
4 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 1991-2023 High School Youth Risk Behavior 
Survey Data. Available at http://yrbs-explorer.services.cdc.gov/.  
5 https://pritzkercenter.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Pritzker-Domestic-Violence-Report-Updated-
April-2025.pdf 

3 
 
of medical examiner data. These deaths accounted for over 40% of the 156 women killed 
during that time6. As a County, we can and must do more.  
This Board has acknowledged that DV/IPV and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) 
prevention must be prioritized and funded two positions in the Department of Public 
Health (DPH) to support these efforts. We allocated ongoing funding to support 
community-based organizations in their GBV prevention work and recently passed a 
motion transitioning the County’s Domestic Violence Council into a new structure to allow 
for greater community membership, participation and accessibility. On July 7, 2026, this 
Board passed a motion7 focused on strengthening domestic violence prevention efforts, 
particularly acts that involve gun owners and the death of multiple family members, 
including reinforced targeted outreach to men and boys. The resulting report back 
detailed the many efforts the County’s Office of Violence Prevention (OVP), housed within 
the Department of Public Health (DPH), has led in this space, and offered several 
recommendations the Board could take to further strengthen the County’s work.  
Since it was established by the Board in 2019, OVP has done work in the DV/IPV 
space. In 2024, OVP formed a workgroup of domestic violence service providers, law 
enforcement agencies, City and County departments, community leaders, survivors, and 
other interested stakeholders to explore how to reduce domestic violence homicides by 
improving access to Domestic Violence Restraining Orders (DVROs) against those 
abusing their intimate partners. In a report issued on July 31, 2024, OVP shared a number 
of recommendations developed by the workgroup, including increasing legal aid, 
centralizing information, embedding a peer navigator model, improving data tracking, 
 
6 https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-16/la-county-restraining-order-data-analysis 
7 https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/218606.pdf 

4 
 
standardizing training, posting informational fliers, co-locating social services at self-help 
center in courthouses, extending Emergency Protection orders, providing information on 
legal rights upon DVRO filing, and standardizing notification of service.  
These recommendations, most of which have not yet been implemented, were 
discussed in a recent Los Angeles Times article,8 which reported that in 2025, LA County 
courts received almost 15,000 petitions for DVROs and dismissed almost 60% of them 
due to procedural delays from the survivor making the request. This is nearly double the 
Statewide dismissal rate. For a DVRO to be enforceable and the hearing for a permanent 
order to be set, the alleged abuser must first be served with a temporary restraining order 
(TRO). The order can be served by law enforcement, a paid registered process server or 
a third party, such as a friend or family member. This step is critical-- of the cases with 
incomplete service in 2025, 70% were ultimately dismissed. The LA County Sheriff's 
Department (LASD) can serve restraining orders but, in 2025, LASD deputies were 
unsuccessful in locating targets of restraining orders almost half the time.  
The County’s DV/IPV work is not, and should not be, isolated to OVP. The County’s 
Department of Business and Consumer Affairs (DCBA) operates the Self- Help Legal 
Access Center (SHLACs) Program, which provides in-person and remote self-help legal 
assistance at nine regional locations throughout the County. The most recent SHLAC 
report9 from DCBA notes that restraining orders continue to be one of the top services 
they provide, accounting for 23% of their workload. Of the 49,092 individuals served by 
the SHLACs, 11,413 obtained or modified an enforceable court order and 10,423 
experiencing mental or physical threats reported feeling safe from abuse and/or threats 
 
8 https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-16/la-county-restraining-order-data-analysis 
9 1218019_2026-09-18SHLACBiannualWorkloadReportNo.34_rc.pdf 

5 
 
of harm as a result of the assistance received. DCBA’s August 2025 report noted that 
62% of all SHLAC’s clients are women10. DCBA has repeatedly asked for and been 
denied additional funding to support the demand for the services provided by the County’s 
nine SHLACs. These services, which support DV survivors at no cost, are often cited as 
a critical support that must be expanded.  
 
We also know that DV and IPV are contributing factors to unstable housing and 
homelessness. The 2026 point-in-time Homeless Count found more than 5,690 people in 
the City of Los Angeles became homeless after fleeing domestic or intimate partner 
violence11. That number rose by more than 43% in a single year. The Count also found 
that over 29,400 people in Los Angeles County reported they had past DV/IVP 
experience, representing 47% of the homeless population over the age of 1812.  Yet in 
the FY 26-27 Measure A budget, County HSH had only 45 beds of DV/IPV interim 
housing, 115 slots of Time Limited Subsidies, and zero units of permanent housing 
dedicated to this population.  
Further complicating support for DV survivors, Los Angeles County does not 
currently have a single centralized hotline that serves as an intake for survivor services. 
Survivors must call individual providers one by one in an attempt to find the resources 
they need, many of which are extremely time sensitive.  The LA Continuum of Care was 
awarded funding for a centralized hotline in 2024, with plans to begin the program in 
January 2025. However, delays from the Department of Housing and Urban Development 
 
10 DCBA-SHLAC-Report-August-2025.pdf 
11 https://www.lahsa.org/documents?id=10075-hc26-city-of-los-angeles-data-
summary&_gl=1*17fxmyp*_gcl_au*MTQzNzcxMTk4Ni4xNzkwMTE5NTYy 
 
12 https://www.lahsa.org/documents?id=10076-hc26-coc-data-summary 

6 
 
have stalled the program's start. A provider was selected to lead this work; they have job 
descriptions and potential vendors identified to stand up the hotline as soon as the 
contract is executed but cannot do so without one-time start-up funding. A centralized 
hotline, paired with the County’s funded Community Information Exchange, will 
transforming the victim service provider network into a working system that reduces the 
time it takes survivors to secure critical life-saving resources.  
The time has come for this Board to take bold action in this space. GBV and 
DV/IPV affect millions of Angelenos and result in real and significant harm, physically, 
emotionally, and mentally. The County must step up and lead in this space, ensuring that 
this work is prioritized at every level.  We need to work together to identify new and 
underutilized funding streams, break down silos between various county departments, 
and work collaboratively as a County to better serve and support survivors and their 
families. We need to think creatively about how to build a better system to support 
survivors, to make access to services easier and more seamless. Our bureaucracy should 
not be a barrier to individuals getting the help they need, begin healing, and feeling seen, 
safe and secure.  
WE, THEREFORE, MOVE, that the Board of Supervisor direct: 
1. The Chief Executive Officer to: 
a. Begin the process to add “Gender-Based Violence and Intimate Partner 
Violence” as a Board-directed priority, using the definition of “Gender-Based 
Violence” previously approved by this Board. The CEO should submit a 15-
day written report back with suggested language around the Board-directed 
priority for Board review.  

7 
 
b. Report back in writing as a part of the FY 27-28 recommended budget with 
sources of ongoing funding for an additional amount of $2 million annually 
for a total of $5.1 million beginning in the FY 27-28 budget to fully fund the 
Department of Consumer and Business Affairs’ (DCBA) Self Help Legal 
Access Centers (SHLACs). This ongoing funding will allow the SHLACs to 
provide additional legal assistance for those in need of applying for 
restraining orders and other legal services by bringing on additional DV/IPV 
specialized providers.   
c. Report back in writing within 14 days with potential sources of one-time 
funding in the amount of $1.25 million that can be used immediately to stand 
up an LA County centralized DV/IPV hotline that would serve as an intake 
for survivor services.  Potential sources of funding should include settlement 
funds and other one-time non-Net County Cost (NCC) funds. 
d. Report back in writing as a part of the FY 27-28 recommended budget with 
sources of ongoing funding in the total amount of $3 million annually 
beginning in the FY 27-28 budget to fund the IPV/DV clinics co-located at 
County Courthouses to provide additional legal aid supports to survivors.  
e. Submit a 60-day written report back on all County investments related to 
Gender-Based Violence and Domestic Violence/Intimate Partner Violence. 
This should include federal, state, and local dollars. This report-back should 
include a comparison with the investments of the City of Los Angeles, 
including investments in the housing space.  

8 
 
2. Request the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department provide a verbal 
presentation to the Board no later than November 24, 2026 on their current efforts, 
staffing and protocol related to serving Domestic Violence Restraining Orders 
(DVRO) and Temporary Restraining Orders (TROs). This presentation should also 
discuss plans to improve service outcomes and any additional resources needed.  
3. DCBA in partnership with Department of Public Social Services (DPSS), 
Department of Mental Health (DMH), IPV/DV providers and existing Family Justice 
Centers to explore how to integrate additional social service supports within 
DCBA’s Self Help Legal Access Center (SHLACs). A written progress report, 
including any challenges and/or required resources, should be submitted to the 
Board in 60 days. This report should also explore how the SHLACs can better 
connect with existing providers, courthouse clinics, and Family Justice Centers to 
ensure all available resources are leveraged and avoid creating duplicative 
systems.  
4. The Office of Violence Prevention (OVP), housed within the Department of Public 
Health (DPH), to: 
a. Report back in 30 days in writing with an update on the County’s existing 
GBV efforts and how they are supporting IPV/DV work throughout the 
County. This report should explore how current efforts could be improved, 
challenges, capacity and resource needs, and opportunities for expansion.   
b. Report back in writing in 60 days on recommendations for implementing a 
Peer Navigator model to support IPV/domestic violence survivors. These 
recommendations should be informed by domestic violence advisory 

9 
 
programs, including the County’s Domestic Violence Coalition, and Family 
Justice Centers. The report should include a discussion of any funding or 
capacity needs to launch the program along with an implementation plan 
and timeline. The report and recommendations should be informed by those 
with lived experience and domestic violence providers, along with additional 
key stakeholders.  
c. Execute and administer a sole source contract with Downtown Women’s 
Center (DWC); and execute further amendments as needed, upon review 
and approval by County Counsel, for the provision of consulting services for 
the implementation of the DV shelter referral component of the Countywide 
Community Information Exchange (CIE), formally CareConnect; in an 
amount not to exceed $462,300.  The CIE platform will facilitate and 
improve access to domestic violence shelter referrals for survivors and their 
families;  
d. Report back in 120 days with recommendations on how survivors can 
receive additional support and guidance throughout the restraining order 
process, especially when service is unsuccessful or hearings are delayed. 
These recommendations should include actionable steps to strengthen 
communication and referral pathways between law enforcement, legal 
service providers, Family Justice Centers, and IPV/DV advocates to ensure 
that survivors are better equipped navigate these challenges while 
maintaining appropriate safety and confidentiality protections. The 
recommendations should be informed by lived experts, IPV/DV advocacy 

10 
 
providers, Family Justice Centers, law enforcement, and other relevant 
stakeholders; and  
e. In partnership with Probation, Department of Mental Health, County 
Counsel, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, and all relevant 
County departments, report back to the Board in 120 days with 
recommendations to improve countywide identification and intervention to 
prevent 
domestic 
violence-related 
murders 
or 
murder-suicides. 
Recommendations should include opportunities to connect perpetrators to 
violence-intervention programs earlier in the law enforcement process and 
strengthen coordination among IPV/domestic violence service providers, 
suicide prevention, behavioral health, law enforcement, courts, and other 
relevant systems. This should include any training, data-sharing, or policy 
changes needed to implement these recommendations. 
WE, FURTHER, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct:  
5. The Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS): 
a. In partnership with OVP, and in collaboration with JCOD, DMH, HSH, 
DPSS, and DHS, report back in 160 days on how the County may be able 
to leverage the Families First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA) funding to 
support families, prevent maltreatment, and reduce system involvement. 
This report back should include a cost-benefit analysis examining whether 
the County should explore FFPSA as a possible source for reimbursement 
funds, and what would be required to ensure current providers and services 
qualify for this federal reimbursement.  

11 
 
b. In collaboration with the Mandating Supporting Initiative and OVP, explore 
how DCFS can begin to offer and contract for targeted and effective 
IPV/domestic violence services to families involved with the child welfare 
system. These services should be provided to families free of charge, in a 
culturally competent manner, and offer specialized support and expertise 
for families with IPV/DV involvement. DCFS should detail how their plans to 
begin offering these services and mechanisms to bring on specialized 
IPV/DV providers in a 120-day report back, and include possible funding 
sources, implementation timeline, and whether any existing contracts can 
be amended to include this specialized scope of work. This work should 
enhance any existing family supports currently offered by the Department.  
6. All applicable County departments work with OVP, and with support from the 
Internal Services Department (ISD), to ensure that DVRO informational fliers 
and/or posters are printed and posted in all County facilities, particularly in 
women’s or gender-neutral restrooms, and contracted agency bathrooms to 
increase access to information. OVP should report back to the Board in writing in 
60 days on a plan, and if additional funding and/or resources are needed. 
7. The Department of Homeless Services and Housing (HSH), in partnership with 
OVP and other relevant partners, to report back to the Board in writing in 60 days 
with an assessment of the funding and number of emergency beds available for 
people and their children or family members fleeing IPV/DV; the funding, beds, 
and subsidies available for stable housing; and the gap between these existing 
resources and the need. This report should also: 

12 
 
a. Include feedback on how this population can be prioritized for existing 
homeless service response services and housing resources;  
b. Consider barriers survivors may face, such as family size, eligibility 
requirements, safety concerns, pets, transportation, and others, when 
assessing housing needs and developing recommendations; and  
c. Provide a budget illustrating funding and resources necessary for the 
County to be able to provide immediate access to emergency housing for 
any person seeking to flee gender-based violence, using motel funds, 
existing site-based shelter, or other solutions.

located at 4328 East 4th Street and 4341 Eagle Street in unincorporated East Los Angeles
