motions.title: STRENGTHENING ACCOUNTABILITY IN COUNTY COMMUNICATIONS SPENDING AND SUPPORT FOR LOCAL, ETHNIC, AND COMMUNITY-SERVING MEDIA
motions.summary: Directs the Chief Executive Officer to evaluate establishing a Countywide framework to increase advertising and outreach through local, ethnic, and community media, informed by New York City's model. It also directs reports within 120 days on advertising spending, funding for an independent academic study, procurement updates, and stakeholder feedback.
motions.backup_text:
AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS HILDA L. SOLIS 
October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
Mitchell 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Horvath 
 
_______________________________ 
 
 
Hahn 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Barger 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Solis 
 
_______________________________ 
Los Angeles County is home to more than 10 million residents and one of the most 
diverse populations in the nation. Residents rely on timely, accurate and culturally 
relevant information to understand changes in government policy, access public benefits, 
comply with new requirements and connect with essential services. Local, ethnic, 
community and hyperlocal news organizations play an important role in this information 
ecosystem by serving as trusted messengers for immigrant communities, communities of 
color, low-income households, seniors and residents with limited English proficiency. 
These outlets provide news and public service information in multiple languages 
and maintain deep, longstanding relationships with the communities they serve. For many 
residents, particularly those who may not be effectively reached through traditional 
government communications channels, these organizations are among the most trusted 
sources of information. At the same time, local and community news organizations face 
significant financial challenges, including declining advertising revenue, reduced 
newsroom capacity and broader structural changes affecting local journalism. 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS HILDA L. SOLIS 
October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
California has also recognized the essential role of local journalism in supporting 
informed communities, civic engagement and access to reliable public information. 
Through the California Civic Media Program, Governor Gavin Newsom and the 
Legislature allocated $20 million in state funding, matched by additional private support, 
to strengthen local journalism across California, including community-based news 
organizations that provide trusted reporting and public information to underserved 
communities. Additionally, the State approved $10 million to fund journalism fellowships 
based out of U.C. Berkeley, $5 million to strengthen the State’s multi-lingual media 
system, and $3 million for ethnic media outreach grants. These investments reflect 
growing recognition of the role local, ethnic, and community news organizations play in 
connecting residents with reliable information. 
At the same time, residents are navigating rapid and significant changes at the 
federal level, including heightened immigration enforcement activity and changes 
affecting public benefits, health care coverage, housing assistance, nutrition assistance 
and other essential services. These developments have increased the need for clear, 
timely and accessible public information so residents can understand their rights, 
determine eligibility and access available resources. 
Effective government communication requires more than producing information. It 
requires reaching residents through the sources they trust, in the languages they 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS HILDA L. SOLIS 
October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
understand and in the communities where they live. Strengthening coordination with local, 
ethnic, community and hyperlocal media organizations can help the County better reach 
residents who may not be effectively served through traditional government 
communications channels. 
In 2020, the Board of Supervisors directed the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to 
evaluate the County's utilization and investment in ethnic and hyperlocal media and 
develop recommendations for integrating these outlets into County communications 
strategies. The CEO's subsequent report found that while most County departments 
utilized ethnic and hyperlocal media for outreach and education efforts, the County lacked 
comprehensive data on advertising expenditures, utilization rates and outcomes across 
departments. The report identified the need for improved reporting, coordination and 
accountability. 
Other local governments have recognized the need for a more coordinated 
approach to engaging ethnic and community media. In New York City (NYC), a 2013 City 
University of New York study revealed that 82% of city advertising funds went to 
mainstream outlets, while community outlets received only 18%. Despite Latinos 
representing nearly 30% of the City’s population, only 4% of funds went to Spanish 
language publications in a one-year period.  In response, NYC mandated at least 50% of 
advertising funds go to community and ethnic media and established the Mayor's Office 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS HILDA L. SOLIS 
October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
of Ethnic and Community Media to serve as a central point of coordination between City 
agencies and the diverse media outlets that serve New Yorkers. The office helps City 
agencies identify and work with ethnic and community media, provides guidance and 
training on engaging these outlets, maintains a directory of media organizations, and 
supports greater coordination of City advertising and communications efforts. New York 
City has also established policies to increase the use of ethnic and community media in 
City advertising and improve transparency around public advertising expenditures. 
New York City's approach provides a potential model for how government can 
better coordinate its relationships with diverse media outlets and use existing 
communications resources to reach residents more effectively. Following the spending 
mandate, NYC advertising allocations to community media outlets outperformed 
expectations reaching 84% of total advertising budgets. Over the five-year period since 
implementation, $72 million has been redirected into the local media ecosystem. A 
centralized approach can give agencies the tools and information they need to identify 
outlets serving specific communities while creating greater consistency in how public 
information and advertising opportunities are shared. 
Los Angeles County has an opportunity to consider whether a similar structure 
could work here. With more than 10 million residents across 88 cities and unincorporated 
areas, the County must communicate with residents across a vast and diverse geographic 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS HILDA L. SOLIS 
October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
area. County departments regularly communicate with residents about health care, public 
benefits, housing, immigration services, public safety, disaster response and other 
essential services. Local, ethnic, community and hyperlocal media can play an important 
role in ensuring this information reaches residents who rely on neighborhood-based and 
multilingual sources. A Countywide framework could provide departments with a more 
coordinated way to identify and engage these outlets while improving the County's ability 
to understand how its communications and advertising resources are being used. It could 
also help ensure that public information reaches the communities it is intended to serve. 
Therefore, in order to strengthen the County's ability to communicate with its 
diverse population, improve the reach and effectiveness of public information, and better 
connect residents with timely, accurate and culturally relevant information, Los Angeles 
County should evaluate the feasibility of establishing a Countywide framework for 
engaging local, ethnic, community and hyperlocal media, informed by approaches used 
by other local governments, including New York City. 
WE, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1. Direct the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), in consultation with the Internal Services 
Department (ISD), Anti-Racism, Diversity and Inclusion (ARDI) Initiative and other 
relevant County departments, including the Office of Immigrant Affairs, to evaluate 
the feasibility of establishing a Countywide framework to strengthen the use of

October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
local, ethnic, community and hyperlocal media for County advertising, public 
information and outreach, informed by the approach taken by New York City's

(PPP) Assessment Tools could be incorporated into County procurement and

October 27, 2026 
AND JANICE HAHN 
Strengthening Accountability in County Communications Spending and Support 
for Local, Ethnic, and Community-Serving Media 
 
 
 
opportunities for local, ethnic, community and hyperlocal media organizations and

motions.title: SD 2: Preserving HIV Prevention Capacity in Los Angeles County
motions.summary: Approves delegated authority for the Director of Public Health to execute nine sole-source HIV prevention contracts totaling up to $2,167,761 through May 31, 2027, using federal supplemental funds. It also authorizes amending 67 existing HIV prevention contracts through November 30, 2026, to expand services.
motions.backup_text:
-
MORE -
MOTION 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
HAHN 
__________________________ 
BARGER 
__________________________ 
SOLIS 
__________________________ 
AGN. NO. 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL 
October 20, 2026 
Preserving HIV Prevention Capacity in Los Angeles County 
For the past three decades, the federal Centers for Disease Control and 
Prevention (CDC) has invested in community-based HIV prevention as an essential 
complement to the work of State and local health departments. Beginning in 1996, 
CDC funding supported HIV testing, health education, and risk-reduction services in 
jurisdictions heavily impacted by HIV, including Los Angeles County (County). Over 
time, these investments expanded to include linkage to care, biomedical HIV pre- and 
post-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP and PEP), training, social marketing and capacity-
building interventions.  
Initially, CDC awarded HIV prevention cooperative agreements to states and a 
limited number of large urban jurisdictions most affected by the epidemic. Over time, 
CDC expanded its funding to additional State and local health departments, while also 
providing direct grants to nearly 100 community-based organizations (CBOs) 
nationwide. In federal fiscal year 2024, CDC awarded $40 million in core funding to 
96 CBOs and their clinical partners, as well as an additional $14 million to 36 CBOs 
conducting targeted HIV prevention activities in disproportionately impacted 
communities. These direct federal investments complement HIV prevention services 
funded by the State and County, helping to sustain a critical network of community-
based providers. 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL  
October 20, 2026 
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
Rather than recompeting these CBO funding programs, CDC has begun 
shifting resources through State and local health departments. On July 14, 2026, CDC 
issued updated supplemental guidance for PS24-0047, which is the CDC’s Notice of 
Funding Opportunity for High-Impact HIV Prevention and Surveillance Programs for 
health departments. This funding mechanism sets the rules and resources for how 
health departments nationwide carry out core HIV prevention and surveillance 
activities. The updated guidance announced noncompetitive supplemental funding for 
health department recipients. Under this approach, instead of continuing direct CBO 
awards, CDC intends to establish a supplemental pool of funding for which health 
departments may apply and, at their discretion, allocate resources to CBOs. This 
change could result in fewer resources than under the current direct funding model 
and would likely end the longstanding practice of CBOs receiving HIV prevention 
funding directly from CDC. The supplemental funding supports one-time expansions 
of HIV testing, surveillance improvements, and PrEP and PEP activities from June 1, 
2026, through May 31, 2027. The Department of Public Health (DPH) received its 
supplemental award on September 11, 2026. The timing of the award, coupled with 
the fact that the supplemental funding was not initially intended to replace funding for 
formerly CDC-funded CBOs, has created challenges in determining how best to 
program these resources while preserving continuity of critical HIV prevention 
services. 
To mitigate the risk of service disruptions, DPH intends to invest a portion of its 
High-Impact HIV Prevention and Surveillance supplemental funding in local CBOs that 
had previously been funded directly by CDC. This investment is intended as a temporary 
bridge, not a permanent replacement for federal CBO funding, to preserve critical HIV 
prevention capacity and maintain continuity of services while DPH conducts a competitive 
resolicitation of its broader HIV prevention portfolio. Bridge funding would continue 
through May 31, 2027, with new contracts anticipated to begin June 1, 2027, coinciding 
with the next CDC HIV Prevention Cooperative Agreement period for the County. 
Maintaining this community-based infrastructure is particularly important given the 
growing intersection between HIV and homelessness in the County. Recent local 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL  
October 20, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
 
 
surveillance data indicate that the HIV rate among people experiencing homelessness 
increased from 23 per 100,000 in 2020 to 32 per 100,000 in 2024, a 39 percent increase. 
Among approximately 1,560 County residents newly diagnosed with HIV in 2024, 16 
percent reported experiencing homelessness during the previous 12 months, compared 
with 11 percent in 2020. This represents a 45 percent increase in the proportion of newly 
diagnosed residents reporting recent homelessness. Many clients served by the 
programs proposed for bridge funding are themselves experiencing homelessness or are 
at risk of losing their housing. 
Allowing these community-based services to lapse during the transition in federal 
funding could create a significant service gap at a time when the populations they serve 
are experiencing increasing vulnerability. Maintaining CBO capacity through May 2027 
will help preserve access to HIV testing, PrEP and PEP, linkage to care, and other 
essential prevention services, while providing the County with sufficient time to establish 
a sustainable, competitively procured HIV prevention network for the next funding cycle. 
I THEREFORE MOVE THAT THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS: 
1. Delegate authority to the Director of the Department of Public Health (DPH), or 
designee, to enter into nine new HIV prevention sole-source contracts, up to a total 
maximum obligation of $2,167,761, effective upon execution approval through May 
31, 2027, utilizing Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) High‑Impact 
HIV Prevention and Surveillance supplemental funds awarded to DPH on 
September 11, 2026.  This authority includes permission for DPH to: 
a. Waive the County of Los Angeles' (County) open competitive solicitation and 
bidding requirements, the requirement to comply with the County's Sole 
Source Policy, and any other applicable County contracting requirements;  
b. Reallocate funds between contract budgets;  
c. Increase or decrease in funding above or below the annual base maximum 
obligation, based on the availability of federal resources, effective upon 
execution of an amendment; and 
d. Execute change notices to the contracts to:  
i. Authorize modifications to the budget with corresponding modifications 

MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HOLLY J. MITCHELL  
October 20, 2026 
Page 4 
 
 
 
 
to the statement of work and/or scope of work, that are within the same 
scope of services, as necessary;  
ii. Make modifications to Contractor’s or County’s administration;  
iii. Change hours of operation and/or service locations; and  
iv. Immediately suspend or terminate any contract upon written notice to 
the contractor for failure to perform and/or fully comply with contractual 
requirements, and terminate any contract for convenience, including 
cancellation without cause and/or in response to federal, State, or 
County budget reductions, upon written notice to the contractor, subject 
to review and approval by County Counsel and notification to the Board 
of Supervisors and Chief Executive Officer. 
2. Delegate authority to the Director of DPH, or designee, to amend any of the 67 
currently existing DPH funded HIV prevention service contracts listed in 
Attachment A, to add additional High‑Impact HIV Prevention and Surveillance 
funding at any amount, as needed, to support expanded services. This authority 
will extend from the effective date of execution through November 30, 2026, and 
is subject to review and approval by County Counsel, and notification to the Board 
of Supervisors and the Chief Executive Officer. 
#          #          # 
(VG)

In recent years, the County of Los Angeles (County) has taken meaningful steps 
to acknowledge and address false historical narratives about the land upon which the 
County sits and strengthen its relationships with Local Tribal Governments. These 
efforts include adoption of the Countywide Land Acknowledgment; development and 
publication of the County’s report examining past, present and ongoing harms against 
Local Tribes; and continued engagement and consultation with Tribal leaders. Together, 
these actions reflect the County’s commitment to truth, healing and reconciliation; 
elevating the stories, cultures and experiences of the original inhabitants of Los Angeles 
County; and building and sustaining relationships with Native peoples and Local Tribal 
Governments. 
 
The Countywide Tribal Consultation Policy (Policy) represents a significant 
milestone in this ongoing work. As the largest public body in the United States to adopt 
a countywide Tribal Consultation Policy, Los Angeles County has an opportunity to 
establish a model for respectful, consistent and meaningful government-to-government 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS 
OCTOBER 20, 2026 
Adopting Los Angeles County’s First-Ever Tribal Consultation Policy to 
Strengthen Government-to-Government Relationships with Local Tribal 
Governments 
 
 
 
consultation with Tribal Nations. The Policy provides both aspirational and actionable 
guidance for how County departments should consult with Local Tribal Governments 
and incorporate Tribal perspectives, knowledge and priorities into County decision-
making. 
 
The Policy applies to consultation with federally and non-federally recognized 
California Native American Tribes identified through the California Native American 
Heritage Commission’s consultation contact list. By doing so, the County affirms its 
commitment to engaging all Local Tribal Governments with ties to the County in a 
manner that respects Tribal self-governance. 
 
Existing federal and state laws require Tribal consultation in a variety of 
circumstances, including land use planning, environmental review, cultural resource 
protection and repatriation activities. While compliance with these legal requirements 
remains essential, the County recognizes that meaningful consultation extends beyond 
statutory obligations. The Policy is organized around five guiding principles that reflect 
the County’s commitment to building and sustaining respectful government-to-
government relationships: respect for Tribal self-governance; relationship building and 
trust; early, meaningful and ongoing consultation; recognition of Tribal knowledge and 
expertise; and accountability and continuous improvement. Together, these principles 
provide a foundation for strengthening consultation practices across County government 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS 
OCTOBER 20, 2026 
Adopting Los Angeles County’s First-Ever Tribal Consultation Policy to 
Strengthen Government-to-Government Relationships with Local Tribal 
Governments 
 
 
 
and advancing responsive decision-making. 
 
In developing the Policy, the County engaged in an extensive stakeholder-driven 
process that included consultation with Local Tribal Governments and collaboration with 
County employees. Tribal leaders and appointed Tribal representatives provided 
invaluable guidance on consultation practices, priorities and experiences working with 
government agencies. Their input helped shape a Policy designed to foster consistency 
while respecting the unique needs of individual Local Tribal Governments. 
 
Adoption of the Policy represents an important beginning rather than an 
endpoint. Meaningful implementation will require continued partnership with Local Tribal 
Governments, development of departmental procedures, ongoing evaluation of 
consultation practices and regular reporting on progress. Through implementation of the 
Policy, the County can continue advancing its commitment to repairing harms, 
strengthening relationships with Tribal Nations, and ensuring Tribal voices are 
meaningfully included in decisions that affect Tribal communities and Ancestral lands. 
 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1. Adopt the County of Los Angeles Tribal Consultation Policy as the County’s 
framework and guiding document for government-to-government consultation with 
Local Tribal Governments;  
2. Direct all County departments to incorporate the principles of the Tribal

Consultation Policy into their policies, procedures, programs and decision-making 
processes, as appropriate, effective immediately;  
3. Direct the Executive Director of the Los Angeles City/County Native American 
Indian Commission (LANAIC) to develop and return to the Board by March 2027 
with a Countywide Tribal Consultation Policy Implementation Guide to support 
successful implementation of the Policy; and 
4. Direct department heads to identify an individual at the management level to

coordinate consultation-related activities; serve as the department’s primary 
liaison to Local Tribal Governments and County implementation staff; and work 
collaboratively to identify and advance departmental priorities, resource needs and 
implementation actions related to the Policy. 
I, FURTHER, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1. Direct the LANAIC Executive Director to oversee implementation of the Tribal 
Consultation Policy and, following adoption of the Implementation Guide, provide 
an annual report to the Board summarizing implementation progress, 
accomplishments and challenges; recommendations for improvement and 
resource needs; and opportunities to further strengthen County-Tribal Government 
relationships;

2. Direct department heads to report annually to the LANAIC Executive Director on 
their consultation-related activities; and 
3. Direct the Internal Services Department (ISD), in collaboration with the LANAIC 
Executive Director, to develop and maintain a centralized County intranet portal to 
support implementation of the Tribal Consultation Policy. The portal shall serve as 
a resource hub for County employees and include, as appropriate, templates,

motions.title: SD3: Improving Health Departmental Integration
motions.summary: Directs County Counsel and the Chief Executive Office to amend County Code and close the Health Agency within 180 days. Additionally, directs the three health departments to report back within 60 days on interdepartmental communication, collaborative projects, and a framework for continued regular engagement.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
 
MITCHELL 
  _________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
  _________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 _________________________ 
 
BARGER 
 _________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
  _________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH   
               October 20, 2026 
Improving Health Departmental Integration 
Individuals have unique health care needs that span across the three Los Angeles 
County health departments: Los Angeles Health Services (LAHS), Department of Mental 
Health (DMH), and Department of Public Health (DPH).  To ensure improved access and 
delivery of healthcare, over the last few years, the Los Angeles County Board and the 
three health departments have explored how to better collaborate and integrate. 
On August 11, 2015, the Board adopted a motion to develop the Health Agency to 
create an overarching structure focused on health integration while preserving the distinct 
functions of the three health departments. The Health Agency model included the creation 
of a budget unit, director, and staff, as well as noting the relationship between LAHS, 
DMH, and DPH, with each department maintaining separate status as County 
departments. The Health Agency structure was formally approved by the Board on 
September 29, 2015, via adoption of a corresponding ordinance in the County code. 
In the absence of a Health Agency Director, on February 18, 2020, the Board 
adopted a motion to transition the Health Agency via a pilot, to the Alliance for Health 
Integration (AHI).  AHI was established as a shared governance team with funding from 

the three health departments. It was tasked with supporting the health department’s 
workforce, building partnerships, and promoting health care access across the County 
while still respecting each of the department’s unique charge and scope. AHI was charged 
with the following priorities: 1) Integrate and develop prevention, treatment, and healing 
services; 2) Improve access to health care; and 3) Improve organizational effectiveness. 
While the Board transitioned from the Health Agency to AHI, the County Code was not 
amended to formally establish AHI. As a result, the Health Agency remains the entity 
codified in the County Code, and the positions and budget structure supporting AHI 
continue to reside within the framework originally established for the Health Agency. 
On March 1, 2023, AHI’s 6.0 staff were transitioned to DMH to address urgent 
operational needs. As AHI was no longer generating expenses, each department 
redirected the funding within their respective departments to fund other existing 
needs. AHI, as an organization unit has remained with no funding or positions.  Board 
action is required to delete the Health Agency/AHI budget unit from the County Ordinance 
to zero out the budget.   
On May 21, 2024, the Board adopted the motion, “Next Steps for the Alliance for 
Health Integration”, directing the Chief Executive Office (CEO), in collaboration with the 
health departments to retain a consultant to conduct an evaluation of AHI and provide 
recommended options for Board consideration.  The recommendations would support the 
collaboration between the three health departments to improve access to comprehensive 
health care.  The report prepared by TurningWest Inc. (Consultant) was included in the 
CEO’s report back to the Board on March 11, 2025.  

The Consultant facilitated 39 individual and group interviews with the Board’s health 
deputies; former AHI staff; LAHS, DMH, and DPH leadership and staff; other County 
departments; and external stakeholders, including representatives from labor and 
community-based organizations. This discovery process found that:  
• AHI was challenged by organizational limitations; 
• There was misalignment between the collaboration needs of health 
departments and the task of AHI; 
• A perception gap exists in how much “collaboration” is occurring; and  
• Effective collaboration requires both formal and informal structures. 
The 
Consultant developed 
comprehensive 
criteria 
for analyzing 
eight 
organizational design options. The options fell across a continuum from the least 
restrictive to the most formal structure and were scored using a Decision Matrix Scale 
(ranging from 0 – 20 points).  The options consisted of the following: 
1. Implement No Change (7 points)  
2. Increase Communication (16 points)  
3. Create Collaborative Forum (18 points)  
4. Establish Collaborative Units within the Health Depts (11 points)  
5. Reinstate AHI as Independent Unit (10 points)   
6. Reinstate AHI Reporting to the CEO (9 points)  
7. Create Supra-Ordinate Structure Over the Health Depts (9 points)  
8. Merge the Health Departments (10 points) 
The report recommends that, in lieu of a formal AHI structure, the three health 
departments establish a collaborative forum, where the three health department directors 

and key staff come together monthly. Since the publishing of the report the three health 
department Directors have increased communication, which transitioned to collaborating 
closely on several important issues. It is unclear how effective increased communication 
has been, or if a formal structure is needed to ensure that the three health departments 
are better leveraging programing, resources and funding, and ensuring that there is no 
wrong door to access services across the three departments.   
During these uncertain financial times, it is critical that collaboration among the 
three health departments and other departments is strengthened to better leverage 
existing resources so that we may better provide healthcare for vulnerable populations.  
Individuals’ unique healthcare needs can only be fully addressed if comprehensive care 
is available and accessible.   
 
I, THEREFORE MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct:  
1. County Counsel to, in the next 180 days, amend the County Code to repeal 
Chapters 2.73 and 6.83, Los Angeles County Health Agency, and any other 
amendments to the County Code necessary to effectuate that change, and return 
to the Board for any additional authorities required; and 
2. The Chief Executive Office to, in the next 180 days, take all administrative and 
budgetary steps necessary to close the Health Agency in a future budget phase. 
I, FURTHER MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct Los Angeles Health 
Services (LAHS), the Department of Mental Health (DMH), and the Department of Public 
Health (DPH) to report back verbally in Health Cluster and in writing to the Board in 60 
days on the extent and effectiveness of existing increased communication among the 
three health departments on efforts to coordinate services, programs, policies, funding, 

data, and operations for populations and priorities that cross departmental 
responsibilities.  The report should include, but not be limited to the following: 
1.  Identify how the three health department Directors and staff are collaborating, and 
the frequency. 
2. A summary of significant collaborative projects. 
3. A framework for continued regular engagement among the three department 
heads and report to the Board in writing biannually on the status of significant 
collaborative efforts, including successes and barriers. The report should include 
but is not limited to notable collaboration with the Department of Homeless 
Services and Housing (HSH), as well as other county departments whose 
responsibilities intersect with health-related funding, populations, services or 
outcomes. 
#          #          #

motions.title: SD3 and SD5: Providing Spiritual Supports to Specialized Populations
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Mental Health, in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer, to hire a Chaplain using mental health realignment funding to collaborate with faith-based and community partners. It also establishes a voluntary faith-based subcommittee focused on the behavioral health needs of individuals experiencing homelessness.

MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL 
___________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
___________________________ 
 
HAHN 
___________________________ 
 
BARGER 
___________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
___________________________ 
 
 
 
 
 
AGN. NO.             
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS LINDSEY P. HORVATH  
October 20, 2026 
AND KATHRYN BARGER 
Providing Spiritual Supports to Specialized Populations 
In the face of life’s most challenging moments, a calm and comforting presence 
can make all the difference — someone alongside you offering a listening ear, thoughtful 
counsel, and spiritual support when you need it most. This presence is often embodied 
by a chaplain. Chaplains are unique in their capacity to serve diverse communities, 
providing pastoral care outside the traditional church. They are often the unsung heroes, 
quietly offering support where it’s needed most, from hospitals, military, schools, and 
beyond. Their work is crucial, impacting lives every day. 
Chaplaincy is a very specialized ministry where the minister serves not in a church 
nor "para-church" ministry, but in an institutional setting. The chaplain ministers not to a 
congregation, but to the public at large and communities. The people who make up the 
communities served by chaplains may vary in geography, culture, and beliefs and 
demonstrate a wide variety of needs, however chaplains are trained to provide spiritual 
support and guidance based what is being requested/accepted by the individual and/or 

 
 
community served.  Chaplains are there to listen, care, and respond appropriately to the 
agenda of the client and/or their community.  
The Department of Mental Health (DMH) has valued foundational work and 
projects that support the intersection between mental/behavioral health services and 
spiritual support.  This work is done through several existing partnerships with Faith-
Based organizations (FBOs) and Houses of Worship (HOW) through the eight (8) DMH 
Service Area Interfaith Collaboratives and the DMH Faith-Based Advocacy Council 
(FBAC).  Additionally, through a partnership with the County Office of Faith-Based and 
Neighborhood Partnership, DMH has collaborated with other County departments on 
faith-based events and information-sharing.  To augment this work, DMH is seeking to 
provide spiritual support services to clients and their family members in need through 
hiring a Discipline Chief to serve as the DMH Chaplain to interface directly operated DMH 
clinics and the community at large and advise the Department on programming. The 
Chaplain will serve as the DMH Subject Matter Expert and advisor on working with Faith-
Based organizations and serve as an ambassador for the Department, while bringing a 
Faith-Based perspective to department programming, services, operations, interface with 
clients, community and community partners. 
The DMH Chaplain will advise the Department on how to better collaborate with 
communities of faith while honoring faith related beliefs and practices in treatment 
programming. The Chaplain will interface with Faith-Based partners, as well as clinic staff, 
clients and the communities that DMH serves through the creation of listening sessions 
and workgroups focused on spiritual support for various specialized populations, such as 
the re-entry population and individuals experiencing homelessness. 

 
 
 
Through the hiring of a Discipline Chief Chaplain, DMH will be uniquely equipped 
to support DMH staff, consumers and their family members, and strengthen Faith-Based 
partnerships that build upon the natural strengths and well-being that come from 
individual spiritual connection and support grounded in faith related beliefs and practices. 
WE, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Department 
of Mental Health (DMH) in consultation with the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) to: 
1. Identify and hire a Chaplain, funded with mental health realignment funding, to 
collaborate with faith-based partners, behavioral health and homeless services 
and housing providers, community and others. 
2. Establish a voluntary faith-based subcommittee under the Chaplain focused on 
the behavioral health needs of people experiencing homelessness. The 
subcommittee 
should 
collaborate 
with 
existing 
bodies 
working 
on 
homelessness in the faith community.   
3. Report to the Board in writing in 90 days, and quarterly thereafter on the status 
of implementing the above, including identified item, specified role and 
responsibilities, associated costs, and challenges and opportunities if any, until 
the Chaplain position and subcommittee have been established. 
 
#          #          #

motions.title: SD1: Addressing the Behavioral Health Needs of Residents Countywide: Improving the Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health’s Communication with Municipal Partners
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Mental Health, in consultation with related departments, to report back in 45 days with a plan to increase direct communication with municipal partners. The plan must outline how residents can access behavioral health services and explain recent legislative and policy changes.
motions.backup_text:
AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS 
OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Addressing the Behavioral Health Needs of Residents Countywide: Improving the 
Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health’s Communication with 
Municipal Partners  
 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
Mitchell 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Horvath 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Hahn

Barger

The Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health (DMH) is the largest in the 
country and provides critical mental health services to County residents of all ages. In 
fact, as of June 2026, DMH saw nearly 238,000 distinct clients over the last year. DMH 
directly operates over eighty-five mental health programs and contracts that provide a 
wide range of services, including outpatient treatment, residential treatment, case 
management, crisis intervention, and medication support, among many others.  
Given DMH’s many programs and range of services, accessing DMH’s services 
and understanding their limitations can be challenging for cities and municipal partners. 
The complexity of the behavioral health public safety net system is further compounded 
by recent systems changes that have shifted the department’s resources and expanded 
the scope of their work. This includes the transition from the Mental Health Services Act 
to the Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) which took place on July 1, 2026. Under 
BHSA, and its mandated expansion of housing and substance use services, DMH has 
had to adapt and modify its programming to align with funding shifts and new rules. The 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS 
OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Addressing the Behavioral Health Needs of Residents Countywide: Improving the 
Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health’s Communication with 
Municipal Partners  
BHSA transition took place at the heels of the implementation of SB 43 at the start of 
the year, which broadened the Lanterman-Petris-Short (LPS) Act definition of “gravely 
disabled” to include severe substance use disorders, and the inability to provide for 
basic personal needs. Meanwhile, the County launched the Community Assistance, 
Recovery, and Empowerment (CARE) Court on December 1, 2023, as mandated by SB 
1338. CARE Court helps people with untreated schizophrenia and other related 
psychotic disorders receive treatment and services via court petitions from family, 
clinicians, and more. These changes have required DMH to enhance training and 
collaboration with essential partners, including the family of individuals experiencing 
severe mental illness, first responders, and clinicians.  
However, amid all these changes, and the many programs DMH currently 
oversees, municipal partners, including cities, Councils of Governments (COGs), and 
city associations do not always know the best pathway to connect their residents, 
including people experiencing homelessness, to behavioral health services. This 
requires increased awareness of DMH’s services and a direct line of communication 
between DMH and municipal partners to better respond to the needs of individuals 
experiencing behavioral health challenges Countywide.  
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Department of 
Mental Health (DMH), in consultation with the Department of Public Health, Substance 
Abuse Prevention and Control, and the Department of Homeless Services and Housing, 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS 
OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Addressing the Behavioral Health Needs of Residents Countywide: Improving the 
Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health’s Communication with 
Municipal Partners  
to report back in 45 days in writing with a plan to increase DMH's direct communication 
with municipal partners. This report should include the following: 
1. A plan to establish ongoing, direct communication with cities, COGs, and city 
associations. This plan should address the need to establish lines of 
communication with both city administrators/managers and elected city officials. 
2. This plan should address the various information and communication needs that 
municipal partners have, including: 
a. Explanation of how County residents, including people experiencing 
homelessness, can receive behavioral health services from DMH; 
b. Explanation of how municipal partners can best access services to assist 
with constituent concerns, including how to help their constituents access 
behavioral health services from DMH; and 
c. Explanation of the current legislative and policy changes in the behavioral 
health landscape and how they are expected to impact local residents. 
3. Any additional resources DMH needs in order to establish these new lines of 
direct communication with municipal partners.

motions.summary: Directs the Department of Children and Family Services and Auditor-Controller to assess foster youth advocacy entities and recommend options to integrate independent ombudsperson services. It also directs County Counsel to analyze juvenile record confidentiality and authorizes the Auditor-Controller to execute Master of Social Work internship agreements.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
MITCHELL 
__________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
__________________________ 
 
HAHN 
__________________________ 
 
BARGER 
__________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
__________________________ 
 
 
 
 
AGN. NO. _____             
 
October 6, 2026 
MOTION BY SUPERVISORS LINDSEY P. HORVATH  
AND JANICE HAHN 
Providing Advocacy and Problem-Solving Support for All Youth in Foster Care in 
Los Angeles County  
In October of 1998, in response to issues with youth having their rights upheld and 
basic needs met while in group home care, the Board of Supervisors established the 
Children’s Group Home Ombudsman at the recommendation of the Civil Grand Jury and 
Commission for Children and Families.  The Children’s Group Home Ombudsman was 
created within the Department of the Auditor-Controller (A-C) to ensure youth placed in 
County contracted Group Homes had access to an independent, objective, and proactive 
advocate to help them solve problems and address concerns that otherwise would be 
unresolved or unnoticed. Additionally, the Children’s Group Home Ombudsman was 
charged with tracking and reporting trends found across reported problems. At the time 
that the office was established, AB12/Extended Foster Care and its associated placement 
options did not exist. 
Now known as the Ombudsperson for Youth in Short Term Residential Therapeutic 
Programs (STRTPs) (Ombuds), this Office serves as an essential resource to youth in 
congregate care, receiving and responding to requests for assistance, serving as an 

independent advocate to help youth navigate the dependency system, as well as helping 
young people resolve problems and exercise their rights under the Foster Youth Bill of 
Rights (FYBOR).  The Ombuds produces a semi-annual report detailing their outreach, 
requests for assistance, and observations about how to improve processes and outcomes 
for system-involved youth.   
While the Board recently directed the Department of Children and Family Services 
(DCFS) to fund the two non-budgeted Children Services Administrator II (CSA II) items 
already included in the ordinance for the Auditor- Controller to allow the Ombuds to extend 
their advocacy, problem solving, and outreach to youth placed in Transitional Housing 
Placements, like Transitional Housing Placement Program for Non-Minor Dependent 
(THPP-NMD),  the vast majority of children and youth in the dependency system do not 
have a local, independent Ombuds serving and conducting outreach to them.  This 
creates disparities in access to advocacy and support and complicates lines of 
communication for youth who need help. All young people in our care, not just those in 
STRTPS or in transitional housing placements, deserve this level of support.  
Professional standards for ombudsperson offices promulgated by the United 
States Ombudsman Association (USOA) require that ombuds must be independent to be 
effective.  Currently, only the Ombudsperson for Youth in STRTPs meets this professional 
standard requirement, since other ombuds functions that support young people– to the 
extent they exist– are housed within the same department as the clients to whom they 
are supposed to provide independent advocacy and support, and under the same chain 
of command as staff who might be the subject of youth requests for assistance. This not 
only impairs effectiveness; it prevents true independence and a sense of safety for young 
people in moments of real vulnerability and need. 

It is critical that children and youth across the Los Angeles County dependency 
system have equitable access to an independent problem solver and advocate, and that 
the County make the process of requesting assistance for youth in vulnerable settings as 
streamlined and easily accessible as possible.  The current system is a fragmented 
system of advocacy, complicating matters and confusing the young people it is intended 
to serve. The County must do everything possible to reduce burdens by streamlining 
ombuds functions for youth in all parts of the dependency system and explore the 
feasibility of doing so under a single organization. 
     WE, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors: 
1) Direct the Interim Director of the Department of Children and Family Services 
(DCFS), in collaboration with the Auditor-Controller (A-C) and the 
Ombudsperson for Youth in Short Term Residential Treatment Programs 
(STRTPs), to report back to the Board in 60 days, in writing on the following: 
a. An assessment of the scope and responsibilities of existing entities that 
address individual advocacy needs and/or grievances, as well as 
systems improvement, for children and youth across the dependency 
system continuum of care. The assessment should include, at minimum, 
the scope and responsibilities of the DCFS youth ombuds functions, A-
C Ombuds Office, System of Care and the TAY Table, Office of Child, 
Youth, and Family Wellbeing, CDSS’s Foster Care Ombudsperson, 
Children’s Law Center, and CASA of Los Angeles;  
b. An explanation of the Ombuds-like requests DCFS currently tracks, how 
that information is tracked, and an analysis of the resources and time it 

would take for DCFS to track their Ombuds information in a way that is 
comparable to how the A-C does their tracking; and  
c. A review of other jurisdictions that have state and/or local foster care 
ombudspersons that includes details on the forms and functions of these 
offices and the means by which child welfare information and data is 
shared between the ombuds office and the child welfare agency.  
2) Direct County Counsel to submit an analysis to the Board, in writing, in 60 days, 
regarding the confidentiality of juvenile case records as applied to information 
sharing between DCFS and the A-C Ombuds Office and/or direct access of 
DCFS systems and databases by the A-C Ombuds Office. This analysis should 
also include guidance on any next steps required to allow for data sharing 
between DCFS and the A-C Ombuds Office.   
3) Direct the Auditor-Controller, in collaboration with DCFS, to report back to the 
Board, in writing, in 90 days, based on the report submitted in response to 
Directive 1, with:  
a. An update on the progress of the transfer and implementation of youth 
ombuds functions pertaining to THPP-NMD and similar settings to the A-
C Ombuds office;   
b. Recommendations for a phased, multi-year approach to better integrate 
the work of the A-C Ombuds office with the work of existing entities that 
address individual advocacy needs and/or grievances for children and 
youth across the dependency system continuum. The recommendations 
should address whether the work of any existing entities may be 

consolidated within the A-C Ombuds office so that there are independent 
ombuds functions for children and youth across the dependency system 
continuum, uplift opportunities for the A-C Ombuds office to collaborate 
with existing entities, and/or explore the need for an expanded scope of 
work for the A-C Ombuds office. The recommendations should also 
include funding and staffing requests should additional needs be 
identified;  
c. Tailored outreach strategies to distinguish and publicize the points of 
access for ombuds services; and 
d. Continued semi-annual written reports to the Board, public, and other 
stakeholders on the activities of the A-C Ombuds Office. 
  WE, FURTHER, MOVE, that the Board of Supervisors direct the Auditor-
Controller to:  
4) Execute agreements for the provision of Master of Social Work field placement 
internship program services and training in basic social work practice under the 
direct supervision of an agency Field Instructor, with no funding required for 
these agreements; and 
5) Approve the extension of these and other local university affiliation/placement 
agreements for internship placement and training as they expire, following the 
appropriate review: University of California, Los Angeles and California State 
University, Dominguez Hills.

motions.title: SD3: Strengthening Partnerships Between DPSS and Community Clinics
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Public Social Services to establish regular meetings and information-sharing processes with community clinics, evaluate clinic communication approaches, and distribute materials promoting self-service options. Additionally, requires a report back in 60 days on implementation progress, call center wait times, and strategies to expand call center capacity.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
 
 
MITCHELL 
  _________________________ 
 
HORVATH 
  _________________________ 
 
HAHN 
 _________________________ 
 
BARGER 
 _________________________ 
 
SOLIS 
  _________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH                              October 6, 2026 
Strengthening Partnerships Between DPSS and Community Clinics 
 
Changes to social service eligibility resulting from H.R.1 and state actions have 
created immense uncertainty and logistical challenges for benefits recipients, County 
departments, community clinics, and the broader community. Changes to Medi-Cal and 
CalFresh are complex, with new eligibility requirements, different implementation 
timelines, and varying impacts across different populations. The Department of Public 
Social Services (DPSS) has been tasked with a tremendous amount of additional work 
and an enormous responsibility to help ensure Angelenos understand these changes and 
can maintain uninterrupted access, whenever possible, to the benefits for which they 
remain eligible. This includes running the “Keep Your Benefits” campaign and 
implementing new systems to ensure as many people as possible maintain CalFresh and 
Medi-Cal coverage; responding to changes for populations who no longer qualify for 
benefits; preparing for more frequent Medi-Cal renewals; liaising with community 
partners; adapting to ongoing changes in federal policy; and training staff on all these 
changes.  
 
 

Community clinics are critical partners in this work. They not only provide direct 
health care services but also help clients navigate the benefits (re)enrollment processes. 
They inform clients about eligibility changes, help them utilize BenefitsCal, and connect 
with DPSS when an issue cannot be resolved through self-service. Clinic staff often call 
DPSS alongside patients and play an important role in helping community members 
navigate changes to eligibility and program requirements. 
 
Regular meetings and formal information-sharing pathways between DPSS and 
clinics can help ensure that shared clients receive consistent, accurate, and timely 
information while reducing unnecessary burdens on both clinic staff and DPSS workers. 
The work of DPSS and community clinics is complementary, and stronger coordination 
can help support residents as they navigate an increasingly complex benefits landscape. 
The influx of benefits changes has also increased demand on DPSS call centers, 
often resulting in longer wait times for callers. Long wait times can create additional 
barriers for residents seeking to understand or maintain their benefits and can increase 
the burden on both callers and DPSS staff.  
As the County adjusts to a rapidly changing benefits landscape, it must ensure 
DPSS and its staff have the supports, resources, and partnerships necessary to 
administer programs as effectively as possible. Strengthening partnerships can create a 
more streamlined experience for residents and improve the work of DPSS and community 
clinics alike.  
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors direct the Department of 
Public Social Services (DPSS) to: 
1) Establish regular, recurring meetings and a formal information-sharing and case-

resolution process between DPSS and community clinics that assist clients with 
benefits navigation; 
2) Evaluate existing materials and approaches used by community clinics and other 
community partners and, where appropriate, incorporate additional effective 
approaches into DPSS communications; and 
3) Develop and distribute materials to increase use of self-service options, including 
information about services that can be completed through BenefitsCal, and to 
increase caller readiness, including a list of materials residents should have 
available before contacting DPSS, broken down by program, while ensuring clients 
who require phone assistance continue to have timely access to it. 
I, FURTHER, MOVE that DPSS report back in writing in 60 days on: 
1) Progress implementing the directives above; 
2) Current data on call center wait time and strategies to increase call center 
capacity to support callers that require phone assistance with an Eligibility 
Worker, including an assessment of opportunities to leverage technology, 
expand self-service options, provide call-back options before callers abandon 
or disconnect, and the resources, staffing, technology, or operational changes 
DPSS would need to implement those strategies.

motions.title: SD-1 • “Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers” for October 06, 2026 Board Agenda
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Regional Planning and partner departments to amend Title 22 of the Zoning Code to define and prohibit large-scale data centers in all zones. Also directs Public Health to evaluate noise regulations and instructs staff to identify necessary funding.
motions.backup_text:
AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
 
 
MOTION 
 
Mitchell 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Horvath 
 
_______________________________ 
 
 
Hahn 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Barger 
 
_______________________________ 
 
Solis 
 
_______________________________ 
Data centers servicing artificial intelligence (AI) consume high rates of energy, 
over-utilize water resources, contribute to environmental pollution, and impact public 
health in ways that are still being understood. Since computers and the internet became 
an integral component of daily life across all industries in the United States, beneficial 
use data centers have been needed to service computer networks for companies and 
store data. However, the rise of artificial intelligence has led to the evolvement of a type 
of data center that can be more expansive in physical size and consumes more natural 
and infrastructure resources, otherwise known as hyperscale or large-scale data 
centers. A race to maintain an international lead in AI modeling and a renaissance era 
for AI technology has spurred the flurry of hyperscale data center development. 
Although the United States (US) ranks 24th in the world in population adoption of 
artificial intelligence at 28.3%, in contrast to countries such as the United Arab Emirates 
(UAE) with a 64% adoption rate, the US still leads in the development of large-scale 
data centers - building more than 10 times that of any other country.1  
Residents across the San Gabriel Valley, and across other areas of the country, 
 
1 https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
have raised significant concerns and sought government involvement for the regulation 
of data centers through moratoriums, bans, and management. In a study by Stanford 
University’s Center for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, only 23% of the public at 
large in the United States expected positive impacts from AI. The same study also 
revealed that globally, the United States ranked the lowest in trust level from residents 
in governments’ ability to regulate AI. 
Locally in Los Angeles County, opposition to data centers has been strong. 
There were 101 pages of public comment received by the Board of Supervisors in 
reference to the motion which primarily called for a moratorium on data centers. This 
has had immense impact on the outcome of responses by local jurisdictions, such as 
Monterey Park, where, in response to a permit application, the City took action to 
prohibit data centers and support a ballot measure as a means of banning data centers 
in their community.  In November 2026, residents of the City of Alhambra will consider a 
ballot measure similar to the City of Monterey Park’s. Other surrounding cities in the 
San Gabriel Valley such as Montebello, Baldwin Park, and El Monte have enacted 
moratoriums on data centers. 
Recently, top leaders in the development of AI have vocalized concern regarding 
the rapid pace at which AI is evolving and expressed a need for stronger safeguards 
due to the immense risk potential for broad impact on communities across the nation 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
should the technology continue at its current trajectory.2 Data centers and AI are 
interconnected and without stronger safeguards and more active intervention leaning on 
caution, a powerful tool can grossly impact our physical world.  
On April 14, 2026, a motion was filed to begin a study to understand potential 
local impacts of data center development in Los Angeles County and to seek 
recommendations by County departments, with a focus on unincorporated areas due to 
the County’s jurisdictional boundaries when creating and enforcing ordinances. The 
motion also directed the County’s Chief Executive Office of Legislative Affairs to track 
and support bills that are intended to regulate data centers. The motion’s report-back 
also included information highlighting the actions of other jurisdictions that range from 
moratoriums (a temporary pause on permit approvals for data centers) to bans 
(permanent pause on permit approvals for data centers) and zoning ordinances.3 At the 
state level, several bills have been submitted and are at varying stages of review. The 
bills include various elements tied to data centers, including protecting residents from 
higher electrical rates, requiring data centers to go through an environmental impact 
review prior to receiving permitting approval, reporting water usage, and more. Across 
jurisdictions, posture towards data centers is leaning towards more restrictions, 
oversight, and involvement by local municipalities. The motion’s report-back additionally 
 
2 https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/12/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-seeks-
immediate-slowdown-artificial-intelligence-01073519 
3 https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/215369.pdf 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
included recommendations from LA County Departments of Regional Planning and 
Public Health regarding next steps. The primary recommendation was for an 
amendment to Title 22: Zoning Code to define data centers, and to prohibit hyperscale 
data centers in all zones.  
Given the pressing concerns to immediately prevent the environmental and 
health effects of data centers powering AI from impacting unincorporated County 
residents, it is imperative that the Board of Supervisors act on the recommendations to 
prohibit these facilities expediently. Additionally, on September 17, 2026, the Director of 
the Department of Regional Planning utilized the authority granted to her in Title 22 to 
rely on the absence of a similarly defined land use to prohibit large scale data centers, 
until any comprehensive amendments to Title 22 of the Zoning Code are completed. 
I, THEREFORE, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors:  
1. Direct the Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning to initiate, in 
coordination with the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, the Chief 
Sustainability Office, Los Angeles County Fire Department, Internal Services 
Department, and Department of Public Works, work on a comprehensive 
amendment to Title 22 of the Zoning Code and prepare a corresponding 
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) analysis that: 
a. Establishes clear definitions for data centers based on acreage, square 
footage, energy use (megawatts), and water consumption, and 
distinguishes data centers by primary use, ensuring hyperscale and 

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
artificial intelligence data centers are made clearly distinct from beneficial 
use data centers, such as enterprise data centers, accessory data 
centers, or sole-source data centers that are meant for daily computational 
use; and  
b. Prohibits all large-scale data centers (as defined by the ordinance) in all 
zones.  
2. Direct the Director of the Department of Regional Planning to engage with 
residents of unincorporated areas to inform them of their action taken to utilize 
authority granted to her in Title 22 to rely on the absence of a similarly defined 
land use to prohibit large scale data centers as described in this motion until such 
time as Directive 1 is completed.   
3. Direct the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, in coordination with 
County Counsel, to evaluate the need for amendments to Title 12, Chapter 
12.08, to address low frequency and continuous noise associated with large-
scale data centers. 
4. Instruct the Chief Executive Office, in collaboration with the Department of 
Regional Planning, to identify the necessary funding to prepare and implement 
the amendment to Title 22 and associated environmental analysis under the 
CEQA described in Directive 1, and, in collaboration with the Department of 
Public Health, to identify the necessary funding to prepare and implement any 
necessary amendments to Title 12, Chapter 12.08.  

AGN. NO.__________ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR HILDA L. SOLIS                                     OCTOBER 6, 2026 
Safeguarding Public and Environmental Health from Data Centers 
 
 
I, FURTHER, MOVE that the Board of Supervisors instruct the Department of 
Regional Planning, in consultation with County Counsel, to be prepared to introduce a 
moratorium prohibiting data centers that pose a serious risk and nuisance to health, 
safety and environmental resources, particularly water and energy resources, when a 
data center is proposed in the unincorporated area of Los Angeles County that presents 
a current and immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare.

motions.title: SD-3 • “Advancing Low-Carbon Construction in Los Angeles County” for October 06, 2026 Board Agenda
motions.summary: Directs the Department of Public Works and relevant departments to report back within six months with recommendations for reducing embodied carbon in County-funded construction projects. Also directs the department to partner with regional entities and the US Green Building Council of California to scale low-carbon concrete use.
motions.backup_text:
MOTION 
 
MITCHELL   ________________________ 
HORVATH  _________________________ 
HAHN            _________________________ 
 
 BARGER  
_________________________ 
SOLIS 
 _________________________ 
 
AGN. NO. _____ 
MOTION BY SUPERVISOR LINDSEY P. HORVATH                              October 6, 2026 
Advancing Low-Carbon Construction in Los Angeles County 
Los Angeles County is a globally recognized climate leader, nonetheless there is 
still substantial room to deliver on our commitments to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045.  
The OurCounty Sustainability Plan (OSP) and 2045 Climate Action Plan (CAP) have 
several goals related to transitioning to sustainable and healthy building design and 
construction, including: 
• Expanding the use of sustainable building materials for County projects, 
including recycled and repurposed material, low-carbon concrete alternatives, 
sustainable pavement, renewable and biodegradable materials, energy 
efficient materials, and locally sourced materials (OSP Action 132) 
• Adopting the CALGreen Tier 1 and where possible, Tier 2 statewide green 
building standards (OSP Action 34). 
• Adopting a concrete code for new construction that limits embodied carbon 
emissions (CAP Action 3.2). 
• Adopt reach code requirements that include performance standards to limit the 
amount of embodied carbon associated with construction (CAP Action 3.3). 

The carbon intensity of a building comes from both its construction and its 
greenhouse gas emissions during operations.  Construction is responsible for 23% of 
greenhouse gas emissions globally, and the embodied carbon from cement 
manufacturing is responsible for an estimated 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions 
through limestone calcination and fossil fuel combustion in the high-temperature kilns that 
heat concrete to 1,400-1,500 degrees Celsius.  The greater Los Angeles region has one 
of the largest concrete markets in the nation, with an estimated 15 to 20 million cubic 
yards of annual demand, the volumetric equivalent of pouring concrete for one Olympic 
swimming pool every two hours 
Several state and local governments have set policy on low-carbon construction 
operations.  In 2019, Marin County adopted a low-carbon concrete ordinance and 
required that all cement meet content or embodied carbon limits.  SB 596 (2021) tasks 
the California Air Resources Board to develop a strategy to reduce the greenhouse gas 
intensity of cement used in California to achieve net-zero emissions by 2045.  In 2022, 
New York City issued its Clean Construction Executive Order directing all City capital 
construction agencies to use clean construction practices and sustainable building 
materials, including specifications for low-carbon concrete through its contracts and 
projects.  In 2024, the City of Santa Monica established Global Warming Potential limits 
and cement reduction mandates for concrete poured in all newly constructed private and 
public buildings.  CALGreen, the State’s green building code, requires large non-
residential and school building products to reduce embodied carbon through various 
compliance pathways including the embodied carbon of building products and materials.  
Strategies to reduce emissions from concrete include use of supplementary cementitious 

materials, plant electrification, alternative binders, carbon capture, utilizing recycled 
concrete aggregates and component salvage.  
In May 2026, the US Green Building Council of California (USGBC-CA) in 
partnership with the County of Los Angeles, City of Los Angeles, and City of Long Beach 
issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking commercially available and emerging low-
carbon concrete solutions. Thirty unique market participants responded, indicating strong 
industry readiness to deploy low-carbon concrete in our market.  The report found 
substantial availability of low-carbon concrete, but barriers for industry to scale – notably 
reliable demand.  The RFI found that most regional cement plants already offer low-
carbon concrete alternatives at or below conventional costs, which are estimated to be 
suitable for roughly 60% of concrete applications by volume.   
This year, Los Angeles County Public Works is managing approximately $3.3 
billion in construction contracts across approximately 130 active capital projects, a 
combination of “horizontal” infrastructure projects like roads, sidewalks, and sewer repair, 
and “vertical” projects including new office buildings, water treatment plants, and 
community centers. The County and our public partners, including Metro, have a 
tremendous opportunity to lead by example, move the market, and significantly reduce 
the environmental impact of construction, while avoiding cost increases.   With the 
continued organization of USGBC-CA, the County should participate in a regional 
partnership across government and industry to collaborate on regional, performance-
based low-carbon concrete standards, pilot project applications and qualified product 
lists, and other strategies to bring lower-carbon concrete to scale. 
 

I, THEREFORE, MOVE that Los Angeles County Department of Public Works 
(DPW), in coordination with the Chief Sustainability Office, Internal Services Department, 
Los Angeles County Development Authority, and other applicable County departments, 
to report back to the Board in writing within six months with recommendations for a 
phased approach for reducing embodied carbon in County-funded construction projects.  
The report should at minimum consider criteria for new construction, substantial 
renovation/maintenance, and use cases for vertical and horizontal construction.  If viable, 
the report should also include regional performance-based low-carbon concrete 
standards, qualified products list, and initial pilot application opportunities, as well as a 
medium-term goal of emissions reduction per concrete poured as part of a phased in 
implementation roadmap. 
I, FURTHER, MOVE that DPW partner with the US Green Building Council of 
California, Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the City of Los 
Angeles, the City of Long Beach, and other interested regional partners to share best 
practices and opportunities for regional harmonization to bring low carbon concrete to 
scale.  
#          #          #
